Live vs pending. Price data runs through the 2026-08-28 close. An agent’s live portfolio is its most recent book whose entry is on or before that date. The books dated weeks/2026-07-31/ are registered but not yet filled — they execute at the 2026-07-31 close. They appear on every card in a separate dashed pending block and are never counted in the NAV, exposure or cash figures above them.

Three things not to misread. (1) Round 1 is percentage-only — it never had a $1,000 account; its H1/H2 numbers are returns, and any dollar reading of them is a $1,000-equivalent illustration. (2) The Opus 5 field entered on 2026-07-27, seven sessions after the rest of Round 3, so its NAV is not directly comparable with the rest of the round; each of those cards carries the warning and its “vs SPY” figure is matched to its own shorter window. (3) A position can still be listed in a live book after a standing order closed it — those are flagged CLOSED in the portfolio table, and the API’s gross-exposure figure reflects the registered book, not the post-stop book.

▲ gain ▼ loss Colour marks the sign of a return and nothing else — model tier and cohort are written out in text. Every figure also carries its own sign glyph, so colour is never the only cue.

(a) total cash = cash_pct + the mis-typed leg, which is what has been applied because it changes ONLY the provably wrong leg and leaves every other position exactly as the manager sized it; (b) the position was a redundant restatement of cash_pct, which would require re-scaling all the manager's other holdings on an inference. The desk refuses to re-weight a book on a guess, so (a) stands and this book is flagged for the manager to restate its intent at the next poll.experiments/round2/weeks/2026-07-31/fleet_haiku_concentrated_ai_technology.json

StrategyConcentrated AI-infrastructure conviction, unlevered, with a small contrarian BTC spot leg and dry powder for weekly dip-buying

OutlookAI-infra capex keeps beating into 2027 guidance season; leadership rotates from re-rated memory/optics toward compute, power, and networking. Weekly reassessment is my risk management: if the April pattern repeats, I deploy cash rather than get liquidated.

Why no leverageMy edge, if any, is name selection in one theme. Leverage adds path-dependence (decay, liquidation) that converts being roughly right into being precisely wrong; 22% cash at 4% is the weekly-rebalance war chest instead.

StrategyRate-cycle rotation + carry + early trend-reversal, with stop discipline

Novelty statementMy R1 and R2 books were both concentrated long AI-infrastructure conviction. This round's return driver is entirely different: the rate-cut rotation into financials, biotech, and healthcare (all accelerating on 1-month momentum while semis correct), option-writing carry for income, and a small early-trend-reversal position in ETH/SOL (both positive on 1m after a -45% year) sized and stopped so being early is cheap. No AI-capex thesis anywhere in the book.

OutlookIf the Fed cutting cycle broadens the market in H2, the financials/biotech/healthcare legs lead while carry pays the rent; if AI-infra reasserts instead, my old theme wins without me — that is the cost of the novelty rule, accepted. Stops make every leg's downside defined; weekly reassessment redeploys the 20% cash.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Checked macro, Fed, and every position. Key findings: (1) AI trade unwinding hard — Nasdaq 100 in 11% correction, record rotation out of AI winners, chip selloff accelerating on China competition and AI-capex-return scrutiny; NVDA ~$197. (2) Fed held 3.5-3.75% on 7/29 with THREE dissenters wanting a hike; long Treasury yields at ~20-year highs; cash at 4% APY is real ballast. (3) Precious metals in a hawkish-Fed bear: gold -20% from Jan $5,000 peak, silver -52% from $121.62 to ~$58 — but silver has stabilized ~2 weeks and sell-side targets ($67-81) sit far above spot, so my R3 metal shorts are mature. (4) Oil war premium deflating: WTI -7.5% to $82.61 on US-Iran de-escalation, EIA sees sub-$80 Q3 / $70 YE — breaks XOP's trend, boosts JETS/IYT fuel economics. (5) KRE rallying with a +52bps 2s/10s steepener tailwind. (6) XBI +24.9% YTD on a $106B biotech M&A wave — momentum intact. (7) GEV beat revenue and raised FY26 guidance ($24.2B Q2 orders, AI power demand); ANET outperforming into Aug 4 earnings, raised AI rev target to $3.5B. (8) BTC ~$64k with hike odds ~36% and 10% APR long funding — contrarian long not confirming. (9) XLI cited as a mid-July sector leader.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: The three-legged macro premise I wrote this book on seven days ago has inverted on two legs and decayed on the third, so holding it would be holding a view I no longer have. (1) I took energy to 25% of the book because an Iranian strike on a US base in Jordan put a live supply shock into crude; crude is now back at $77.08 WTI / $82.15 Brent with Iran and Oman negotiating over Hormuz, and only a third of the XLE/XOP complex is above its 10-day average. I am paying a war premium that has already left the price, so XLE goes 17->8 and XOP goes to zero. (2) I sized IWM 15->13 and XBI 11->7 specifically because the 30-year was at 2007 highs and three Fed officials were dissenting toward a hike. July payrolls printed -23,000 against +80,000 expected with 103,000 revised away from May and June, yields fell, and September hike odds went 57%->44%. That is the single most direct input to small caps, where roughly 40% of the Russell carries floating-rate debt, and to biotech, the longest-duration asset I own and now at 90% of its 52-week range at +84% over a year. Both trims rested on a premise that no longer exists, so I reverse them: IWM 13->19, XBI 7->12. (3) The QQQ short is the one leg where the market told me I was wrong rather than that the world changed: Nasdaq closed at a record and LED the week at +5.2% against the S&P's +3.6%, so the equal-weight-over-megacap spread ran against me. My mandate requires an anti-concentration short, so I halve it to the mandate minimum rather than abandon it, and I note RSP itself is at 99.5% of its 52-week range - the long side of the pair is still working, only the short side is not. Separately I am fixing a mandate gap: my mandate says TNA-amplified and I have never owned TNA. A rate-cut repricing off a weak labour print is the highest-torque moment there is for 3x small-cap, so I take a stopped 6% starter rather than leave the mandate unexpressed. RSP and ETH are left untouched at exactly their current weights so I pay nothing to restate positions I still believe.

SOXL was unchanged (136.81 -> 136.81) across four days in which SMH gained +0.42%, and lost 40.4% in a month SMH lost 9.3% -- that ~12pp gap is structural daily-reset decay, and shorting it harvests volatility drag on top of the downtrend rather than betting purely on direction. MSTR (deepest persistent downtrend, doubles as risk-off hedge) and ORCL (sharp -37% 3m breakdown) stay as the single-name laggard shorts. Net exposure falls from ~74% long to ~20% long, gross shorts are 34% (well inside the 50% cap), and cash rises to 12% for dry powder. Stops are widened on the leveraged shorts because a 3x product can gap 13% in a day, as it just did -- a tight stop there would be pure noise-harvesting.

  4. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    Free information falsified two of my five longs and one of my four shorts, so the momentum mandate itself demands a rebalance. GS is out: it fell 5.09% in a session and sits 15% below its high, which disproves my recorded thesis that it was the lowest-volatility momentum anchor, and it was always the loosest fit to a software/semis/fintech mandate. HOOD is out: down 42% from its high and at just 29% of its 52-week range DESPITE a record quarter (revenue $1.31B +32%, EPS $0.62 versus $0.43 expected). A momentum leader that cannot rally on a blowout beat is not a leader. CRWD trimmed 12->7 on decaying relative strength (71% of range, 17.5% off its high). SNOW upsized 8->13 as the new anchor: 96% of its 52-week range and UP 4.64% on a day the Dow lost 1,000 points, the strongest relative-strength reading available to me. PANW held at 12. MSTR short covered entirely - the most important thing I learned: Strategy holds ~843,775 BTC worth roughly $54B against a $34B market cap, so mNAV has flipped below 1.0, BTC is +6.33% on the month, the company has paused buying and built $3.75B of cash, and it reports today. The premium-collapse mechanism that drove the -45% is spent, and shorting a levered bitcoin claim trading below its asset value into a catalyst is bad risk. I also trim rather than press the two shorts that already paid: SOXL 12->10 after a single -16.02% session (that is where squeezes start, and JPMorgan is already calling for a buying opportunity), and ORCL 6->5 because it sits exactly on its 52-week low of $114.50, 66% off its high, against a $248 consensus target and a fresh $7B defence contract.     Stated reason (desk log)

    Momentum means following the trend that exists, not the trend I wish existed - and the trend has inverted hard. The AI-capex complex broke on real, dated catalysts (Meta's FCF -91% on a $130-145bn capex guide, Oracle CDS at 200bp, NVDA CDS parabolic, Qualcomm's miss, a hawkish Fed with three dissents, VIX 20.66). MTUM itself is -15.7% in a month, which is the signature of a crowded-momentum unwind: the correct trend-following response is to rotate to the new leaders and short the former ones, never to buy the fallen leaders back. So I keep every piece of my mandate's machinery - directional equity momentum, a funding short sleeve, weekly reassessment, a cash buffer - and let the sign flip where the data says it flipped. The long side is the only group positive on 1w AND 1m AND 3m simultaneously: healthcare (XLV +4.3/+3.4/+16.1), staples, defense on post-earnings drift (RTX +10.5% 1w, LMT +10.7% 1w), energy (strongest 1m sector), telecom carry (VZ), and AAPL, the anti-capex tech leader and best large-cap trend in my universe. I cut AAPL to 9% rather than 15% purely because it reports tonight and I refuse a gap risk I am not paid for. The funding sleeve is no longer short crypto - BTC 1m is now +2.6% and ETH +9.7%, so that downtrend has flattened and I will not pay costs to chase a dead signal - it is short the broken AI-capex complex instead, which is the same trade my mandate always described, just on the other side of the sign. ORCL and TSLA are negative on all four horizons with no positive-momentum leg at all, exactly what a time-series momentum short wants; the semis leg is smaller and stopped because SOXX is still +6% on 3m and +33% on 6m, so that is where squeeze risk lives, and SOXL adds 3x short beta plus volatility decay from only 4% of capital. Net beta lands near 0.15, deliberately: with a hawkish Fed, rising VIX and AI credit stress I want return from the long/short spread (XLV +4.3% vs SOXX -16.3% in one week) rather than market direction. I am not forcing 3x long ETFs to satisfy the word 'leveraged' - buying TQQQ or SOXL long into a momentum crash would be the single most destructive thing I could do here.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: My short sleeve was built on one explicit claim, which I wrote down: hyperscalers are trapped, because cutting capex collapses orders and keeping capex gets the stock hit like Meta's was. Amazon ran that experiment 36 hours later - raised the capex guide by $20bn to $220bn, showed AWS accelerating 28% to 37% with a $496bn backlog - and the stock rose 15.6%. Microsoft did the same on Azure and rose 16%. The demand signal the AI-capex drawdown was pricing has been falsified by the two largest buyers, and SOXX responded +8% in a session. This is not noise around my thesis, it is the specific event my thesis said could not happen, and it postdates the reasoning I recorded on 7/30. Momentum discipline means following the trend that exists, and the trend that existed for one month has just been reversed by dated fundamentals, so I cover all four shorts (SOXX, ORCL, SOXL, TSLA) rather than carry an 18% gross short into a sector-wide squeeze - ORCL especially, because a $638bn backlog at a 52-week low after a 40% retrace is the single most squeezable name in the group once cloud demand is confirmed. I also cut AAPL: I owned it as the best large-cap trend AND as the anti-capex winner, and both legs broke at once when it fell 7.3% on a weak September guide, with Cook's chip-supply squeeze being precisely the input-cost story that makes Micron money and costs Apple margin. So I express that same insight on the correct side. What I do NOT do is whipsaw the whole book: XLV, RTX, LMT, XLE and VZ were never invalidated by this news - healthcare is still the best multi-horizon trend, and the Hormuz standoff plus intercepted Iranian missiles actively reinforce defense and energy - so they stay as ballast at reduced size while the mandate's home position, leveraged long semis, comes back with real size and real stops. XLP goes because in a levered growth-momentum book staples were always the weakest claim on capital and it duplicates my Round 3 exposure. Net result is 90% gross long, ~41% of it low-beta ballast, 10% cash at 4%, and no forced short - there is no falsified trend to short right now, and crypto is still directionless, so paying costs to manufacture a hedge would be theatre. Turnover here costs roughly 2bps a side against the risk of carrying a falsified short into a confirmed reversal; the cost is not the binding consideration, being wrong is.

Over the same week the rest of the complex did the opposite: SOXX and SMH rallied hard, semis ETFs topped weekly fund flows for the first time, and the Nasdaq closed at a record 26,690 after a -23,000 payroll print repriced the Fed dovish and pulled the 10-year to 4.64%. So this is not risk-off to be hidden from, it is one sub-sector breaking while the mandate's core is being confirmed, and the honest momentum response is to move weight out of the falsified driver and into the trends actually making new highs. MU goes from my top weight to a residual tail rather than to zero, because it fell only ~1.2% while peers fell 17% - 40% of its bits sit under $22bn of long-term contracts, so it is the relative-strength survivor of a broken sub-sector, which is worth a small position and not a large one. I add TQQQ because the record high was Nasdaq-wide and rates-driven, not chips-only, and my mandate names that instrument. XLV comes down because it was ballast bought when the semis reversal was still unconfirmed and that doubt has now been resolved; VZ goes entirely because carry ballast is a worse buffer than the 4% cash I already hold. XLE is trimmed because a labour market shedding jobs is a demand-side negative that leaves the leg resting on supply premium alone.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The trend this mandate rides inverted, and the reason is macro rather than idiosyncratic, so momentum discipline says cut leveraged beta and raise cash rather than average into a break. SMH went 588 -> 560.42 (-4.7%), Nasdaq -2.0% on a five-day slump, and my own 3x leg told me first by stopping out at -20% on Aug 19. The mechanism is that the 30-year Treasury printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, on fiscal supply and tariff/energy inflation - a term-premium repricing, not a growth scare. Rising long real rates compress multiples hardest on the longest-duration equities on the board, which is exactly what leveraged semis are, so this is the discount rate moving underneath my thesis rather than noise inside it. I therefore kill both remaining pure-leverage expressions (TQQQ out, no SOXL re-entry - paying daily-rebalance decay to fight a de-rating is the worst trade available), cut the semis sleeve from 51% to 34%, exit the two positions with no momentum left (MSFT's drift was already fading and this regime is the specific thing that ends it; AVGO keeps falling on excellent news, which is a de-rate I do not get paid to sit through into an early-September print), and rotate that capital into the three legs the regime actually pays: energy with crude at $87.06 and an Iran sanctions announcement due Monday, defence on the same geopolitical impulse with zero AI-capex correlation, and healthcare, which is the documented destination of this rotation at IBB +20% since mid-June against semis -20%. Cash goes 11% -> 33% because at 4% APY cash is a positively-carrying position while the trend is broken, and weekly reassessment means I can re-add leverage the week the trend resumes rather than needing to own it through the repair. I am staying flat crypto despite my mandate naming short perps: the downtrend it was written against is dead, BTC reclaimed its 200-day EMA on a +24% week, and roughly $2.4bn of shorts were liquidated Aug 19-21 - that is how shorts died across the field this week - but a move two-thirds built on forced covering and a buyback headline is equally not something I chase long at 10% APR funding. Flat is the honest position, not an omission.

At a 4.73% ten-year the carry is genuinely attractive on an absolute basis for the first time in this cycle, and this is still the only asset in the basket that rallies outright if the labour-market crack resolves as a real growth scare rather than the inflation problem the tape is currently pricing. Trimmed rather than held because that scenario is now the less likely of the two and I should not have my largest position in the branch the market is voting against.

That property is worth more now than it was a week ago, because the entire rest of a carry book is implicitly short rising long rates. Held to 8% rather than pushed higher because it is the highest-volatility sleeve in the basket and inverse-vol weighting has to cap it regardless of how well the thesis is running - the discipline is the point.

Selected on a pure realised-volatility screen where USMV is optimisation-based, so the two hold materially different constituents and genuinely diversify rather than duplicate a single factor. Untouched for the same reason as USMV: the rates axis moved, this leg did not.
HYGequitylong6.0%—−6%noneCut 8% -> 6%, continuing the direction I have been trimming rather than reversing it. Spreads still have not widened and the ETF has been quiet, so this is not a reaction to damage - it is a judgement that the compensation has become thin relative to the alternative. Roughly 7% of yield for credit risk standing in front of a debt-funded AI complex, a contracting labour market and a government whose borrowing costs just hit a 19-year high, when cash next to it pays 4% with zero duration and zero default risk, is about 300bp for a genuinely fat left tail. Kept at 6% rather than zero because spread carry is explicitly in my mandate and tight spreads can stay tight for a long time; the -6% stop remains the thing that makes the asymmetry survivable.
XLREequitylong6.0%—nonenoneCut 9% -> 6%, the largest reduction among the equity carry sleeves, because REITs are the most rate-sensitive asset I own outside the Treasury complex - they are levered vehicles whose cost of capital is the long yield that just hit a 19-year high, so they take the hit twice, through the discount rate on the cash flows and through refinancing. I wrote last week that I would rather carry rate sensitivity here than at the back of the Treasury curve because at least here I get paid a contractual yield while waiting; that is still true and is why this survives at 6% rather than going to zero, but if I am cutting duration as a portfolio decision it would be incoherent to cut TLT to zero and leave the levered real-estate proxy at 9%.
XLPequitylong6.0%—nonenoneHeld at 6%. Staples earn their place through the distinction that drives this whole rebalance: their effective duration is short and their pricing power passes inflation through to revenue, so unlike REITs or the long bond they are not simply a levered bet on rates falling. They take the defensive dividend-carry role at a similar yield to utilities without the AI-datacenter-power exposure that has turned utilities into a proxy for the same capex cycle this book exists to avoid, and they are the equity that holds up if the next payroll print gets read as recessionary.
KOequitylong5.0%—nonenoneHeld at 5%. The single-name expression of defensive dividend carry with the strongest trend of any staple and a stable, growing dividend, and it shares the inflation pass-through property that is the reason I am keeping staples while cutting the pure bond proxies. Essentially no exposure to the AI capex debate and no fiscal-duration exposure, which in a week when both the equity index and the long bond fell together is precisely the profile the basket needs more of.
Tequitylong4.0%—nonenoneTrimmed 5% -> 4%. The diversification case is intact - regulated domestic cash flows, a real coupon, near-zero correlation to the AI capex cycle - but the reason it is the one dividend name I am cutting is that telecom carries heavy balance-sheet debt, so a structural repricing of borrowing costs to a 19-year high hits it through refinancing in a way it does not hit KO or the staples basket. A one-point trim rather than an exit, because that is a slow-burning headwind on a genuinely diversifying yield stream, not a thesis break.

  4. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The carry book has done its job - flat at +0.05% with a -0.75% max drawdown while the Nasdaq entered correction - but three of its four carry sleeves have stopped paying and I would rather fix them now than collect a coupon into a drawdown. First, duration is not being paid: TLT -4.9% on 1m and IEF -1.7%, with the Fed on hold against THREE dissents and Warsh talking hawkishly. Term premium is a thesis about being compensated for rate risk, and right now I take the risk without the compensation, so TLT goes entirely and IEF stays only as the genuine risk-off hedge if this AI unwind becomes a growth scare. Second, the insight I actually care about: XLU is no longer a bond proxy. It was quietly repriced over the past year as the AI-datacenter-power trade and is now unwinding with the rest of it - SRE -5.4% 1m, AEP -6.2%, XLU -2.4% 1m. Holding it as a 'defensive low-beta income' sleeve means holding hidden AI beta inside a book whose entire purpose is not to have any, so it goes and its income role passes to XLP, KO and T, which carry similar yield with actual positive momentum and no capex contamination. Third, GDX at -16.9% on 3m and -32.7% on 6m is not convexity, it is leverage pointed at a downtrending asset; I take the +4% bounce since the book was set and exit. I also cut SPY, because inverse-vol balancing says the equity risk premium should come from USMV and SPLV, up 2%+ on the week while SPY fell 2.4%. HYG comes from 15 to 11 with a tight stop: high yield still pays its ~7% coupon, but with NVDA's CDS parabolic and Oracle's at 200bp the AI complex's debt is the fattest tail in credit and I want a defined exit rather than a thesis. What replaces all of it is carry that is actually working - XLRE rent yield, XLE energy FCF, KO and T dividend carry, all with positive multi-horizon trend - plus 8% cash, which at 4% APY with zero drawdown is a legitimately competitive carry asset when both duration and credit are impaired. Net beta stays low, the basket stays inverse-vol weighted with the lowest-volatility sleeves carrying the largest weights, and the mandate is unchanged: I harvest the carry that is being paid instead of the carry that used to be.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: The book is working as designed (+2.20% with a -0.75% max drawdown), so this is a surgical weekly rebalance along one axis the market moved, not a rebuild. The axis is that real assets paid and nominal duration did not: GLD ran +7.3% from Aug 4 and XLE +7.7% on the week, while IEF was -0.14% and TLT -0.87% and HYG was flat with spreads still not widening. I reinstated TLT one week ago on a Fed-reaction-function call, and the specific structure I flagged when I capped it at 6% - that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness fixes - is exactly what showed up, with the long end lagging the belly by 73bp in five sessions. So I cut the long end by more than half, add a point each to the two real-asset sleeves the tape rewarded, and move a point to cash, which yields 4% risk-free and is the cheapest carry available when nothing else is signalling. IEF stays at 15% untouched because one flat week is not a falsification of a multi-week reaction-function thesis and it remains the only sleeve that rallies in a genuine growth scare. Gross drops 92 to 91, which lowers portfolio variance - the direction an inverse-vol mandate should move when its highest-vol bond sleeve stops paying.

  7. 2026-08-24REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-24/opus_momentum.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-24/opus_momentum.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The one axis that moved is the exact axis I wrote my framework around, and it moved violently enough to require extending that framework rather than merely reapplying it. Two weeks ago I capped TLT at 6% on the argument that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness can fix; last week I halved it to 3% when TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%; this week the 30-year printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, and TLT closed $82.05, a 22-year low. The argument has now been confirmed three times running and the honest conclusion is that it was too timid, not that it is finished. So TLT goes to zero. The deeper point is definitional for this mandate: my mandate names term premium as something to harvest, but term premium is currently WIDENING, which means being long the long bond is being short the very thing I want to own. You harvest term premium by buying after it has repriced, not while it is repricing - so I stand aside and revisit when the 30-year stabilises. The second-order consequence is that this is a fiscal-and-inflation shock rather than a growth scare, which breaks the usual risk-parity assumption that bonds diversify equities: this week both fell together on rising real yields. That is why the diversification budget moves to gold, which returned +5.4% on the week to $423.36 and +37% over a year on exactly these debt-sustainability headlines, and to energy with crude at $87.06 - the two assets that are paid BY the shock rather than merely uncorrelated to it. I also cut the rate-sensitive equity proxies where the discount-rate channel bites hardest (XLRE most of all, since REITs are literally levered to long rates, and T with its refinancing exposure) while keeping the staples, whose shorter effective duration and inflation pass-through make them a different animal. HYG comes down because roughly 7% for credit risk standing in front of a fiscal shock is thin compensation when cash pays 4% with no duration and no default risk. Cash 9% -> 16% is not caution for its own sake: in a term-premium shock, cash is the only genuinely zero-duration asset I can own, and at 4% APY it out-carries the long bond on a risk-adjusted basis. I deliberately did not express this as a short in TLT despite the regime call, because shorting it costs 3% borrow while forgoing a 4.76% yield - about 7.8% a year of negative carry against me - and a carry mandate should not pay 7.8% to be directionally right. Holding cash is the same view with positive carry. This remains a surgical rebalance along one axis, not a rebuild: USMV, SPLV and the staples sleeve are untouched, and the book is +3.17% with a -0.75% max drawdown precisely because I keep doing it this way.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I set Thursday's book on the premise that the market had switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE, and that premise was falsified within hours of my decision by a print I could not see: Amazon raised 2026 capex to $220B from $200B, said it still cannot meet demand, and was rewarded +15%, taking the four hyperscalers to $720-745B for 2026, +77% y/y. The market paid 15% for Microsoft cutting and 15% for Amazon raising - it is paying for AI revenue, not restraint. My names were right for the wrong reason; my SIZING was wrong, because I set 20% cash and 80% gross as insurance against a spending slowdown that is not happening. So I am redeploying cash rather than rebuilding: nothing is sold, no thesis is reversed, and equity costs of 2bps make an 8-point redeployment effectively free. Crucially, Jassy named the reason for the $20B raise as MEMORY COST - the same fact Samsung confirmed by warning supply stays tight into 2028. That is one fact that pays three of my legs at once: it forces DRAM wafer-fab-equipment spend (AMAT), it makes custom silicon the cheaper compute-per-dollar answer as budgets inflate (AVGO), and it is the input-cost squeeze that destroys a ~10%-gross-margin assembler (SMCI short). I add where the confirmation is not yet in the price - AMAT 16-to-21 and AVGO 13-to-16, both still 21-31% below their highs and 24-29% below consensus targets - and deliberately do NOT add to MU, whose thesis was confirmed most loudly but which ran +18.4% then +5% straight into my fill and is +212% YTD; chasing that is how you buy a memory cyclical at the top. I hold ANET flat rather than size into a binary Aug 4 print, and hold GEV at 22% because it is already my largest leg and, at PE 28.3 and within 17% of its high, it is no longer the discount it was. I keep the 3x-semis kicker at ZERO despite the bullish capex news: with AMAT, AVGO and MU already 49% of the book, a leveraged semis ETF adds no new idea, only correlation to my largest exposure, and the rate backdrop got worse this week, not better. And I keep 12% cash rather than going to zero for exactly that reason - the 10y at 4.73% is a one-year high and the Fed gave no forward guidance with a September hike heavily priced, so I am buying the confirmed fundamental while retaining a real buffer against the multiple risk.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two things broke my book's logic this week and both point the same way. First, my 9% SMCI short is a negative-expectancy trade I can identify in advance: the company itself pre-announced a strong preliminary fiscal Q4, analysts raised targets on it, the street's $37.81 target sits ABOVE the $31.13 spot, and it closed +5.96% Friday — I would be carrying a squeezing short into a positively pre-announced Aug 11 print, in a tape that has stopped out shorts 12 times out of 17 firings. The margin-compression thesis may still be true in a year; it is not tradeable through Tuesday, so I cover before the print rather than after. Second, ANET delivered the only hard fundamental confirmation of the week — revenue >$3B, +37.7% y/y, full-year guide RAISED to $12.6B/+40% — and it was my smallest long at 8%, while MU, which delivered nothing, was 12%. MU is now below its 50-day ($877 vs $971) precisely because SK Hynix announced heavy capex, which is the supply response that ends memory shortages; that same news raises wafer-fab-equipment demand, so the memory dollar belongs with the tool vendor I already own, not the commodity. I therefore cut MU to a 5% stub (kept only because forward PE 6.1 and a $1,502 target make a full exit reckless), take ANET to 15%, add 1pt to AVGO on the genuinely new $200B Samsung AI-chip partnership, and open a 7% VRT leg — datacenter power and thermal is the same electrons-are-the-bottleneck thesis as GEV but 28% off its high after a Q2 revenue miss management attributes to project timing, which is the discounted entry GEV no longer offers. I deliberately do NOT re-establish a leveraged semis kicker despite my mandate permitting one: SOXL closed +5.99% on Friday and my max drawdown is already -14.61%, so buying 3x semis after a 6% day is exactly the risk my mandate caps. StrategyRotate out of US mega-cap/AI into a soft-dollar basket of international value, commodity-linked EM, energy carry and gold, with a small dollar short.

Pulled full price/trend history (1d/5d/1m/3m/6m/12m plus 50d & 200d moving-average position) for ~60 tickers via Yahoo chart data through the 2026-07-29 close. WebSearch budget was exhausted and most news sites returned 503/403, so the read is built from price action, which was unusually unambiguous.

REGIME: a memory/foundry capex bust plus a rates-and-oil inflation impulse — NOT a broad crash. MU -35.5% 1m, INTC -37.8%, AMD -20.4%, TSM -17.7%, SMH -20.2% (-14.1% in 5 days, -4.8% on 7/29). But NVDA only -2.5% 1m, AVGO -0.6%, MSFT +6.0%, AAPL +20.0%, META +4.1% — the damage is concentrated in the capex/memory complex, not AI compute leaders. SPY just -1.6% 1m, equal-weight RSP +1.3% 1m and +6.0% 3m, HYG -1.0% (no credit stress). VIX 20.7, +24% on the week. This is a rotation out of one crowded trade, not a systemic event.

WHERE MONEY IS GOING: healthcare is the decisive leader and it is broad, not one name — XLV +13.9% 3m/+23.9% 12m, VHT +14.3% 3m, LLY +29.5%, ABBV +24.6%, MRK +19.4%, JNJ +15.5%, UNH +13.5%, IBB +11.8%, PPH +11.4%, IHI +7.9% in 5d. XLV sits +6.8% over its 50d and +9.2% over its 200d. Also bid: staples (XLP +3.5% 1m, KO +7.8% 1m/+13.1% 3m), dividend-quality (SCHD +6.0% 1m, +15.2% 6m, +26.0% 12m, +12.4% over 200d), energy (XLE +9.5% 1m, +18.1% 6m), financials (+5.5% 1m).

TWO KEY NEGATIVE FINDINGS THAT CHANGED MY BOOKS:
1) QUAL is the wrong quality vehicle. MSCI USA Quality is heavy in exactly the megacaps de-rating: -0.6% 1m versus XLV +3.4% and SCHD +6.0%. It delivered tech beta, not defense. SCHD's ROE/FCF-and-leverage screen is the same quality factor without the AI-bubble exposure and it beats QUAL on every horizon.
2) Gold is broken, and so are bonds. GLD -22.1% 6m, -4.1% below its 50d and -9.9% below its 200d; GDX -16.7% 3m, SLV -22.3%. The +2.7% gold pop on 7/29 is a bounce inside a confirmed downtrend. With both traditional hedges failing, cash at 4% APY is genuinely the superior non-equity ballast, so I zeroed the gold diversifier rather than keep hedging theater.

ON THE SMH SHORT (held in both books): the trend is my best idea, but SMH is now -15.5% below its 50-day while still +12.4% ABOVE its 200-day and +70% over 12 months. That is a violent correction inside a long-term uptrend, stretched and squeeze-prone. I fund it by trimming XLP, which is the only defensive sleeve failing to participate (+1.96% over three months). Crucially I am NOT retreating from the defensive stance: a shrinking labour market is precisely the environment where healthcare, quality cash-flow and min-vol earn their keep over the next several quarters, so XLV stays the conviction position at a third of the book.

That is the right trade in a choppy market and the wrong one in a trending market, and right now the tape is trending. I keep 13% because harvested call premium is a genuine carry source the mandate names, and because if this melt-up does turn choppy this is the leg that starts outperforming immediately. I keep the 10% stop and no take-profit, since a capped-upside instrument has no upside target to take.

Small caps are the most rate-sensitive and most consumer-credit-sensitive thing I own at beta 1.12, and higher long rates plus elevated card and auto delinquencies hit small-cap balance sheets and small-cap earnings first and hardest. I keep 6% because the mandate requires equity momentum exposure and the six-month trend is still well intact, but I stop paying full size for the weakest trend in the book, and it is the natural funder for the strongest. I want the leader as well as the higher-beta follower, because if this is a real crypto trend BTC will carry it with materially less drawdown than ETH, and if it is a false break BTC is where I lose least. Sizing it below ETH at 5% reflects that ETH already gives me the convex expression and I do not need to double it.     A trend-and-carry book must exit trends that have broken. MTUM (20%) and JEPQ (20%) were 40% of the book levered to the US mega-cap/AI-infra complex, and the released data shows that complex unwinding: TQQQ -12.69% 1-month and -5.23% on the week, SOXL -40.41% 1-month, SMH -9.33% 1-month with a -3.27% single-day break on 7/24 after mid-week gains — a failed rally, the classic signature of a momentum top rather than a dip. I keep the crypto trend engine unchanged (35bps round-trip makes churn there genuinely expensive and no crypto information was released), raise DBMF to 22% because managed futures is the one sleeve that monetises the new downtrend instead of fighting it, swap JEPQ for JEPI to preserve the option-writing carry while dropping the Nasdaq concentration, cut MTUM to a 8% stub, lift commodity roll carry slightly, and add a 7% short in SMH so the book trades with the dominant trend rather than against it. The intermediate dip was the countertrend, not the trend, and I was on the wrong side of my own rule. Third, the redeployment. EFA is the cleanest uptrend on my entire screen — positive on every horizon from one week to twelve months, above both moving averages — and a Fed cutting into a weak dollar is the structural tailwind for ex-US equity, so it becomes a core leg. IWM gets the equity-momentum slot: 13.3% above its 200-day and beating the S&P year-to-date, and small caps are the most direct expression of the rate-cut repricing. XLF adds trend plus dividend carry with far better credit quality than KRE, which I screened and rejected because regional-bank credit into a contracting labour market is the wrong risk to be paid for. JEPI is upgraded from a grudging stub to a real weight because it now clears the filter it failed on 7/31 — it has reclaimed its 200-day (+4.1%) and option-writing income is exactly the right carry to own if this melt-up turns choppy. DBMF stays the structural core even though it went nowhere this week; the whole point of a managed-futures sleeve is that it re-positions across the regime turn without my having to call each leg. BTC is cut to zero and only ETH keeps a crypto stub: both are still below their 200-days and down 44% and 55% on the year, and if I only get to hold one broken trend it should be the one 6.7% above its 50-day rather than 2.6%.

Second, a genuinely new carry signal appeared where I was not positioned: copper spreads are at their highest since 2021, which is backwardation paying actual positive roll yield, against record prices driven by AI and grid demand into constrained supply.     Weekly desk 2026-08-22: A trend mandate that cuts a leg for failing confirmation is obliged to add it back when confirmation arrives, otherwise the rule is not a rule. Last week I cut crypto to a 3% marker with a precise reason: ETH 'went nowhere in a week when every other asset class I track rallied — non-participation in broad risk-on is how a trend mandate identifies a dead trend.' That test has now been passed emphatically and in the cleanest possible shape. ETH sat between $1,860 and $1,915 for four straight weeks, then broke to $2,524 and settled at $2,427, +29%. BTC sat between $62.8k and $65.0k for three weeks, then went $64.7k, $69.4k, $73.1k, $78.3k and settled at $77,227, +20%. Long consolidation base, decisive break, shallow 1.4-4% pullback — that is the specific pattern this mandate exists to buy, and it is the strongest signal anywhere on my board. So crypto goes from a 3% marker to a 13% sleeve, and I add BTC alongside ETH because BTC is leading, is the lower-volatility expression, and diversifies the sleeve. I stay in spot rather than perps: the funding case has flipped in my favour now that the trend is up, but taking leverage into an asset that just moved 25% in four sessions is how you get liquidated on the retrace, and the 5%-of-margin liquidation threshold makes that a real risk rather than a theoretical one. Funding comes from the two weakest trends and from cash. IWM is the one leg that broke down rather than paused — it printed 305.18 and faded to 299.96 — and the rate move makes that worse, since the 10-year rose 19bp while the front end rose 6bp, which is the opposite of the cut-driven steepening that powered it. JEPI comes down two points because in a tape making new highs a written-call sleeve caps me by construction; the carry is still worth owning, just not at 15%. CPER gives back a point after fading 2.4% from its high. Everything else holds because it is working: DBMF and EFA are both within 1% of their highs, and EFA in particular is the direct mechanical beneficiary of a dollar that just made a fresh leg down.

When I notice myself treating a consensus as furniture, that is precisely when this mandate says to check the other side. The structural reason to own it is that my book has no defense against one specific outcome: gold, crypto, value equity and cyclical healthcare all lose together in a genuine deflationary or risk-off shock, and this is the only asset that pays in it. I size it at 7% and accept that it is falling, because the warning from my backtests was that shorting momentum kills portfolios — a long in an oversold asset with a bounded floor is the opposite risk shape.

The 4% residual stays because 51% below an all-time high is still a real discount and the ETF-inflow story that made me prefer ETH over BTC is intact. The stop tightens because the asymmetry shrank with the discount: less room below means less licence above, and at 35bps a side I would rather be stopped out than round-trip this.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the biggest thing wrong and the cost of admitting it one session in is about 0.2bp, so I am admitting it. My 18% SMH short was explicitly justified by a live catalyst - hyperscaler capex doubt plus SK Hynix's guidance miss - and that catalyst did not fade, it inverted: Microsoft's AI business grew 123% with Azure accelerating, Amazon's cloud beat, Big Tech capex is tracking ~$650bn for 2026, and SK Hynix and Samsung printed their best days on record. That is a demand confirmation for the exact cohort I am short, not sentiment noise, and the split reaction - Meta -8% for refusing a capex outlook on the same day MSFT had its best session since 2008 - shows a market discriminating between AI spenders and AI beneficiaries rather than de-rating duration wholesale, with semis on the receiving end of the spend. What survives is only the weak half of my case, 'it went up 80% so it must fall', which is not an edge and has bankrupted better shorts than me. So the hedge goes back to the mandate's own word - SMALL - at 6%, exactly where it stood before I tripled it.     Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Three names have had their theses actually falsified by news this week and one had its thesis confirmed while the price fell, so I am reallocating along the evidence rather than sitting still. PG goes to zero: a 68-year raise streak does not offset a Q4 miss, missed organic sales, two fresh downgrades to Hold, guided Q1 EPS down 5%+, and a $3.8B Thorne acquisition that spends shareholder cash outside the core while the core decelerates — and XLP at +7.18% over a year against XLV at +29.17% says the entire complex is dead money. ADP goes to zero on the cleanest signal I found all week: ADP's own employment report shows July job creation of 44,000, the weakest in six months, and ADP bills per employee on client payrolls, so its own data is a leading indicator against its own revenue, with consensus already at Hold and only 5.66% upside. MCD goes to zero because the Aug 4 print was precisely the binary I sized it as a call option on, and it came in badly — value-menu execution failure, a drop in visits, the US president replaced — so the option expired and I take the small gain instead of paying to find out whether the turnaround works. Against those cuts I add ABBV, which beat at $3.65 vs $3.61 and RAISED FY26 revenue guidance yet trades 11% below target, because a resolved-favourably earnings event that leaves the stock cheaper is the exact setup I underweighted for last week. I open MDT, a 48-year aristocrat at a 3.30% yield and 0.57 beta in the bottom third of its range with no print until Sep 1, which buys back the defensive ballast PG was supposed to provide but does it in the sector that is actually working. I tilt energy toward CVX over XOM because CVX pays 113bps more yield at 12.2x forward with 16.3% upside versus 10% for the same oil-price driver. Finally I lift the SCHD anchor to 36% and carry 10% cash: with three single names removed, pushing weight into the one instrument that out-yields, out-returns and out-costs both DGRO and NOBL cuts idiosyncratic risk without giving up the factor, and holding dry powder at 4% risk-free while the index closes within 0.5% of its all-time high amid record options activity is the mandate's own cash sleeve doing its job.

The book gained 3.36% in four days and in doing so spent most of its own upside: every leg now sits in a 4.7%-10.7% band to consensus. Two legs no longer clear the bar for what they cost me. XOM goes to zero because it is now the worst position on both axes my mandate cares about, 2.57% yield and 5.28% upside, against CVX at 3.56% and 8.48% off the identical crude driver; my entry thesis already said every dollar in a fixed energy budget is better spent next door, and I only paid for a second operator because both had double-digit upside — that premise is gone. JNJ goes to zero because it is a duplicate function, not a bad company: I hold it purely as low-beta ballast, and MDT does that identical job at 0.57 beta with 154bp more yield and 3.2x the upside, so owning both is paying twice for one role — and JNJ specifically has the lowest yield in the book at 2.06%, cut FY26 EPS guidance again, and keeps deploying cash outside the dividend into Firefly Bio and a $2.58B Sail deal. CVX is trimmed rather than exited because it is my best performer and that is precisely the issue: the Middle East geopolitical premium I flagged at entry as one-headline-reversible has now been banked as a 7% gain while the risk turned into an actual headline, with Trump publicly attacking Big Oil profits and demanding pump-price cuts. I bank part of it and keep 7% for the second-highest yield in the book. The freed 13 points go where the evidence is strongest: 4 to SCHD, because when single-name upside compresses everywhere the right home is a 103-name quality-income basket at 3.04% yield and 0.06% fee rather than another idiosyncratic bet; 2 to MDT, which took a UBS upgrade to Buy on an explicit turnaround call and now absorbs JNJ's ballast role; 2 to ABBV, still the widest gap in the book at 10.74% upside, sized up only two points rather than more because the pending Apogee deal did cut FY26 EPS guidance and that is a real demerit against my entry note. The remaining 5 points go to cash at 15%. That is a considered position, not residue: with the median upside in my entire universe now around 8% and a 3.36% gain already in hand, 4% risk-free is a competitive return, and my mandate names harvesting that cash yield explicitly. I also pulled every take-profit down to just above where the sell-side actually is — +18% on CVX, +15% on ABT and MDT and ABBV were set against wider gaps and would now simply never fill, which is the same correction I made to KO last week.

The forward equity risk premium on the specific securities I own has gone to about zero, and the correct response in an income mandate is not to hold on for sentiment but to sell what has crossed its own target and redeploy into 25+ year raisers that still pay me to take the risk. ABT is the cleanest case: at 2.37% upside and a 2.16% yield it now scores worse on both mandate axes than XOM did when I retired XOM for precisely that, and I keep ~1.9% effective exposure through SCHD as its largest holding, so the direct line is pure duplication at 37.7x earnings. ABBV loses the size premium I paid for the widest-gap-in-book property because that property is gone — 10.74% upside became 4.39% in five sessions. KO is at its 52-week high on 26.8x forward for a 2.33% yield. Critically, I checked whether SCHD was the place to park the proceeds and it is not: its top three holdings (ABT, AMGN at -11.57%, MRK at -3.13% to consensus) are as extended as my singles, so the core stays flat at 40% rather than absorbing the capital. Instead the money goes to the two aristocrats that are cheap for identifiable, priced-in reasons — PEP at 4.13% and 16% off its high, O at 5.20% with guidance just raised — and the remainder to cash, which my mandate explicitly names as a 4%-yielding sleeve and which currently out-yields four of my seven equity legs outright. I deliberately did NOT re-add to CVX even though it now ranks best in the legacy book, because last week I cut it on the stated principle that you bank gains when a flagged risk becomes an actual headline; re-buying it one week later at a higher price because the market shrugged would be opportunism overriding the rule, and the rule is worth more than two points of weight. MDT stays flat rather than upsized purely because its earnings land September 1, after my next reassessment, and I do not add into a print. Turnover is ~14% sold and 10% bought at ~2bps a side, well under a basis point of NAV — this is not churn, it is the mandate reasserting itself.

Point-in-time research as of the 2026-07-29 close (web search budget was exhausted, so I pulled live quote/return pages directly).

MACRO REGIME EVENT, 29 Jul 2026: Fed held at 3.50-3.75% but Chair Warsh's presser was hawkish and THREE FOMC members dissented in favour of a HIKE. Dow fell 1,000+ points; 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest level since 2007. Separately, Iran struck a US base in Jordan and crude jumped ~6-7% (USO +7.32% on the day). Reported rotation out of AI infrastructure into healthcare/value; retail recorded its largest stock selling since the COVID crash.

CROSS-SECTIONAL MOMENTUM SCAN (last / 1-day / distance below 52wk high / 1yr total return):

KEY INFERENCES.
(1) SEMIS: best trailing 12m number in the market (+73.6%) but the trend is NO LONGER INTACT. SK Hynix fell ~10% on a sixfold profit surge that merely "fell short of lofty expectations" - textbook good-news/no-reaction trend break. AI-capex sustainability is now the dominant narrative. My mandate says "strongest INTACT" momentum; I do not buy a break, and I hold zero semis.
(2) GOLD MINERS: +40.9% YTD looks like momentum but price is 37% below its 52-week high. Dead trend masked by a stale YTD print. Rejected.
(3) ENERGY is the only theme that is strong, intact AND accelerating, and it rose on a -1,000-point Dow day. Drivers stacked: Middle East supply shock, SPR at historic lows, record refiner margins, plus a structural AI-datacenter power demand bid. XLE is only 7.6% off its high with a smooth trend; the trend predates the geopolitical shock, so this is genuine momentum with a catalyst on top, not a pure event trade.
(4) VEHICLE CHOICE within energy: I deliberately weight XLE (unlevered, -7.6% from high) far above ERX (2x, -17% from high). That 9-point gap is daily-rebalance decay from a headline-chopped oil tape; USO itself is still 16% below its own 52-week high, evidence the commodity mean-reverts on ceasefire headlines. So the leverage sleeve stays small.
(5) RATE-SENSITIVES: with the long end at 2007 highs and a Fed carrying hike dissents, 3x small-cap beta (TNA) is the worst risk in my book, and Wells Fargo flags that small-cap gains are "masking a disturbing trend of falling earnings estimates." Cut TNA, IWM, IWD.
(6) XLF is the weakest name I own on every horizon (YTD +4.4%, 1yr +8.5%). A momentum book must sell its laggard. Cut to zero. KRE is a different animal - 2.5% off its high, P/E 13.4, steepening curve helps NIM - so it survives, trimmed.
(7) XLV is 1.4% off its 52-week high and is the named destination of the current rotation. Best risk-adjusted intact trend available. Upsized.
(8) XBI: +71.6% 1yr keeps it in the book per mandate, but it is 10.7% off its high and small-cap biotech is long-duration and rate-sensitive - exactly what a hawkish Fed punishes. The healthcare bid is going into large-cap pharma (XLV at highs), not XBI. Halved rather than cut.
(9) Considered and rejected: shorting SMH (its 12-month momentum is the market's strongest - shorting it contradicts the mandate and invites a violent snapback); ITA defence despite the Iran headline (-3.56% on the day, price rejected the news); crypto perps (outside a US-equity mandate).

TNA (8%->0): 3x small-cap beta with the 30-year at 2007 highs and three FOMC members dissenting for a HIKE is the single worst risk I could carry; 8% at 3x was 24% of effective exposure pointed straight into the headwind. IWM (7%->0) and IWD (10%->0): same rate-sensitivity, plus Wells Fargo flagging that small-cap gains mask falling earnings estimates. XBI 15%->7%: the mandate keeps me in biotech on its +71.6% 12-month trend, but it is 10.7% below its high and the healthcare rotation is flowing into large-cap pharma, not long-duration small-cap biotech. KRE 14%->10%: still 2.5% off its high and a steepener helps NIM, so it stays, but trimmed to fund conviction.

    WHAT I BACKED. Energy goes from 15% to 54% nominal (~60% effective). It is the only theme in my scan that is simultaneously strong (+37.3% 1yr, +33% YTD), intact (7.6% off high) and accelerating - and it printed +1.88% on a day the Dow fell 1,000 points. The trend predates the Iran strike, so the supply shock is a catalyst layered onto working momentum rather than the whole thesis; record refiner margins, the SPR at historic lows and AI-datacenter power demand all sit underneath it. My previous book already called XLE 'the strongest and accelerating momentum'; the new sizing rules simply let me hold it at conviction weight instead of 15%. Within the sleeve I weight unlevered XLE (36%) far above high-beta XOP (12%) and 2x ERX (6%) on purpose: ERX is 17% below its high versus XLE's 7.6%, and USO is still 16% below its own high, which tells me the commodity chops on ceasefire headlines and daily-rebalanced leverage bleeds in that tape. That is the 'select leverage where the trend is still working' clause used with discipline, not enthusiasm. XLV goes 12%->18% as the highest-quality intact trend on the board (1.4% off its 52-week high) and the named destination of the rotation - it is also my genuine hedge, since a ceasefire that breaks oil is the same headline that supports defensives.

    MANDATE FIDELITY. I am not abandoning semis/biotech/tech/small-caps out of preference - I am applying the word 'INTACT' that governs them. Semis have the market's best trailing 12-month return (+73.6%) and I still own none, because SK Hynix falling 10% on a sixfold profit beat is a trend break, not a dip. Biotech stays at reduced size. The themes rotate; the momentum rule does not.

    Cash 11% earns 4% APY and is real dry powder if oil gaps down. Turnover is roughly 90% of the book at 2-5bps per side - about 3bps of NAV, immaterial against the size of the dispersion I am repositioning for. Stops are widened on the volatile energy legs so a single ceasefire headline cannot stop me out of a trend I still believe in, and tightened on low-vol XLV where -8% would be genuine trend damage. No intraweek_date: the catalyst is live and I want the next close.

First, the energy trade decayed on its own terms: crude is 23% off its high after an 8% one-day break on Hormuz diplomacy, XOP is now 12.6% below its high and ERX 20.3%, and XLE fell 1.13% on a day the S&P closed within half a percent of a record. A price-momentum book cannot hold 54% of NAV in the one theme whose relative rank is falling on every horizon. Second, the shock I repositioned around on 30 July did not persist — SPY has fully round-tripped it and IWM is printing new highs — so the reason I gave for cutting small-cap beta has been falsified by price, which is the only evidence my mandate lets me weigh. Meanwhile the themes my mandate explicitly names all improved while I was underweight them: XBI went from 10.7% to 5.0% below its high with its 12-month return rising from +71.6% to +83.6%, SMH is +104% over a year and turning up, and IWM is at highs. Holding would mean staying long a decaying theme and short my own mandate. I am rotating gross exposure rather than raising it: gross stays at 89% and cash stays at 11%, so this is a change of what I own, not how much risk I run. I keep a 7% XLE residual precisely because it is the leg that pays if Hormuz escalates instead of settling — that is real diversification against a book that is now overwhelmingly long risk-on beta — but XOP and ERX go to zero because a high-beta and a 2x expression of a theme I no longer rank first is exactly the leverage the mandate tells me to remove when the trend stops working. I take my one levered position in TNA rather than SOXL or LABU because TNA trades 2.8% below its own 52-week high against 53.6% for SOXL and 16.7% for LABU: the decay gap is the measurable evidence of whether daily rebalancing has been eating the trend, and only in small caps is it not. Turnover is roughly 55% one-way at 2-5bps a side, about 1.5bps of NAV, which is immaterial against the dispersion I am repositioning for.

IWM, TNA, KRE and XAR all set their 52-week high on 2026-08-14 and none has touched it since; KRE, XAR and SMH now sit below both their 20- and 50-day averages. Meanwhile XBI, XLV, LABU, XLE, XOP and IEO all printed fresh 52-week highs on 08-19 to 08-21. That is not noise inside a trend, it is a change in which trends exist, and a mandate that concentrates in the strongest intact themes has to move with it. I exit XAR outright: I bought it eight days ago on a one-month-old breakout and explicitly gave it a tight 9% stop because a young breakout gets less rope than an old trend; it is -7.51% with 1.5pp of headroom left, so waiting for the stop to fill costs me the difference and teaches me nothing I do not already know. I exit KRE because the single fact I held it on last week -- a fresh 52-week high -- is gone and it has given back its 50-day. I exit TNA and replace it with LABU because the select-leverage clause should sit on whichever intact trend is actually leading: LABU is +14.7% on the week at 91% of its range above all three moving averages, TNA is -5.21% and its underlying peaked on the 14th. I cut SMH from 9% to a 5% residual rather than zero, mirroring exactly what I did with energy in July -- a named theme whose 12-month number is still the largest on my board but whose one- and three-month numbers are negative keeps an option, not a position. The two adds are where the highs are: biotech, and energy via IEO. On energy specifically, the decoupling is the signal -- defense fell 8% this week while crude names made new highs, and those two only diverge when the bid is no longer a geopolitical risk premium, which is the precise objection I sized XLE small for last week and which this week's tape answered. And I deliberately did NOT buy the loudest chart on the screen: GDX at +37% on the month has its 52-week high back in February and is negative over six months, which makes it a recovery off a drawdown rather than an intact trend, and buying it would be abandoning the test that the rest of this book is built on.

Pulled live quotes, valuation stats and news for every line in the book (stockanalysis.com), plus SMH and QQQ for sector/market context. WebSearch budget was exhausted at session start, so all research was done via direct WebFetch of quote and key-statistics pages.

KEY FINDINGS (July 29, 2026 closes):
- MSFT $390.54, but +8.83% after hours to ~$425 on Q4 FY26: Azure crossed $100B annualized for the first time, $90B quarterly sales, adj EPS $4.74 vs $4.24 consensus, and capex guidance MAINTAINED at $175B for CY2026. Fwd PE 21.1, PEG 1.37, ROIC 28.3%, +$20B net cash, 3yr EPS growth est 18.1%, target $555 (+42%). Caveat noted: part of the capex/EPS math comes from extending datacenter depreciation lives from 15 to 25 years — an earnings-quality flag — but the $175B absolute spend and the Azure revenue are real.
- SMH $504, -4.79% ON THE DAY, semis described as "entering bear-market territory"; JPMorgan calls it a summer buying opportunity, Morgan Stanley warns of a harder 2H26. Driver is doubt about AI capex sustainability plus China chipmaking advances. QQQ -2.04% on the day after the Fed held rates steady.
- NVDA $190 (-3.55%), ~20% off its $236.54 52w high. Fwd PE 19.07, PEG 0.43, ROIC 104.7%, +$40.4B net cash, FCF $119.1B at a 47% FCF margin, 74% gross margin, FY26 revenue +65.5%. Consensus target $302.83 (+59%). Earnings Aug 26.
- GOOGL $336.71, ROIC 24.9%, +$121.7B net cash (largest in the book), fwd PE 25.3, PEG 1.77, target +27%. Being penalized for AI capex — the exact thing MSFT was just rewarded for.
- AVGO $370 (-2.78%): PEG 0.51 and a reported >$200B Samsung AI-chip partnership through 2030, BUT net cash is NEGATIVE $45.3B. Fails the explicit "net-cash" leg of my mandate.
- AAPL $338.19: fwd PE 37.1, PEG 3.22, 46-analyst consensus target $321.66 — BELOW the current price. Sitting near its $344.57 52w high after briefly touching $5T. Reports July 30 after close (Tim Cook's last call). Worst risk/reward in the book by a wide margin.
- LLY $1210: retatrutide hit on two Phase 3 trials (~49.6 lb weight loss, files Q1 2027) — genuinely good news, but ~40x with only +5.5% to consensus target and net debt. Novo suing over ad claims. Reports Aug 5.
- COST $974 at ~45-49x for ~10% earnings growth, +11% to target; June comps +8.8% and digital +20.9% are accelerating, but the price is rich.
- V $368.73: Q3 beat, net revenue +14% to $11.6B, FY26 guidance raised for the second straight quarter, 2,600-person AI-driven workforce reduction. Fwd PE 25.5, beta 0.75. MA $563 reports July 30.

CONCLUSION: The semis selloff and the MSFT print contradict each other. The mandate says buy wide-moat, high-ROIC, NET-CASH compounders after a semis/mega-cap pullback — the pullback deepened, so the entry improved. Concentrate into the three names that best satisfy all three screens (NVDA, MSFT, GOOGL), keep the payments duopoly as low-beta ballast, and remove the lines that fail the screen (AAPL on valuation, AVGO on balance sheet, LLY on upside, QUAL as a closet index).

    Why concentrate now: semis are in bear-market territory (SMH -4.79% on July 29) on doubts that AI capex is sustainable — while the largest AI capex spender on earth reported the opposite the same evening. Microsoft put Azure through $100B annualized, beat EPS $4.74 vs $4.24, MAINTAINED $175B of CY26 capex, and traded +8.8% after hours. Those two facts cannot both be right. I am taking the side the evidence supports, which is also the side my mandate was written to take.

    NVDA to 26% (from 8%) is the single best expression of the mandate available anywhere: forward PE 19.1, PEG 0.43, ROIC 105%, +$40B net cash, $119B FCF at a 47% margin, 74% gross margin, 20% off its high, consensus +59%. MSFT to 23% (from 13%): 21x forward with 18% EPS growth, net cash, and the AI-monetization question just answered in its favour; I note the depreciation-life extension from 15 to 25 years as an earnings-quality caveat and it is why MSFT is sized below NVDA despite the cleaner catalyst. GOOGL to 20% (from 12%): the largest net-cash balance sheet in the book at $122B, 25% ROIC, and it is being punished for exactly the capex MSFT was rewarded for.

    What comes out and why. AAPL to zero: PEG 3.22, forward 37x, and the 46-analyst consensus target of $321.66 sits BELOW the $338 price, at a 52-week high, into a binary earnings print tonight — that is the clearest bad-value line I own. AVGO to zero: PEG 0.51 is attractive and the Samsung deal is real, but net cash is MINUS $45B, which fails an explicit leg of my mandate; NVDA gives me the same AI-semis exposure with better growth-adjusted value, four times the ROIC and a genuine net-cash balance sheet, so consolidating rather than splitting is both more disciplined and higher conviction. LLY to zero: fine business, but ~40x with only 5.5% to consensus target and net debt is not a compounder trade, it is dead money with drug-litigation and Aug 5 event risk attached. QUAL to zero: a quality-factor ETF is diversification for its own sake once caps are lifted, and it largely re-owns names I hold directly. COST trimmed 10% to 4%: the June comp acceleration (+8.8%, digital +20.9%) is genuinely good, but ~45x for ~10% earnings growth earns only a token slot.

    V and MA held at 10%/11% deliberately. At 69% in three correlated AI mega-caps I want a real second engine, and the payments duopoly is one: beta 0.75, consumer payment volumes rather than datacenter capex, and Visa just beat and raised FY26 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, which also de-risks MA's July 30 print. 6% cash earns 4% APY and cushions the drawdown I am accepting by concentrating.

    Standing orders: consistent with a hold-to-year-end mandate I am attaching NO take-profits — the whole point is to let compounders compound — and no stops on the ballast, because a stop on a quality book sells precisely at the panic low. The one exception is a deliberately wide 30% stop on NVDA. That level is below the 52-week low, so it cannot whipsaw me on ordinary semis volatility; it only fires if the thesis genuinely breaks (China displacement or an actual AI capex collapse).     Unrestricted-retail resize (2026-07-30, free internet + no sizing caps): The book was ten roughly-equal lines, which under the old caps was forced diversification, not conviction. With caps gone I am sizing to the actual quality screen rather than spreading. The screen is my own mandate: wide-moat, high-ROIC, NET-CASH, bought into a semis/mega-cap pullback.

    Why concentrate now: semis are in bear-market territory (SMH -4.79% on July 29) on doubts that AI capex is sustainable — while the largest AI capex spender on earth reported the opposite the same evening. Microsoft put Azure through $100B annualized, beat EPS $4.74 vs $4.24, MAINTAINED $175B of CY26 capex, and traded +8.8% after hours. Those two facts cannot both be right. I am taking the side the evidence supports, which is also the side my mandate was written to take.

    NVDA to 26% (from 8%) is the single best expression of the mandate available anywhere: forward PE 19.1, PEG 0.43, ROIC 105%, +$40B net cash, $119B FCF at a 47% margin, 74% gross margin, 20% off its high, consensus +59%. MSFT to 23% (from 13%): 21x forward with 18% EPS growth, net cash, and the AI-monetization question just answered in its favour; I note the depreciation-life extension from 15 to 25 years as an earnings-quality caveat and it is why MSFT is sized below NVDA despite the cleaner catalyst. GOOGL to 20% (from 12%): the largest net-cash balance sheet in the book at $122B, 25% ROIC, and it is being punished for exactly the capex MSFT was rewarded for.

    What comes out and why. AAPL to zero: PEG 3.22, forward 37x, and the 46-analyst consensus target of $321.66 sits BELOW the $338 price, at a 52-week high, into a binary earnings print tonight — that is the clearest bad-value line I own. AVGO to zero: PEG 0.51 is attractive and the Samsung deal is real, but net cash is MINUS $45B, which fails an explicit leg of my mandate; NVDA gives me the same AI-semis exposure with better growth-adjusted value, four times the ROIC and a genuine net-cash balance sheet, so consolidating rather than splitting is both more disciplined and higher conviction. LLY to zero: fine business, but ~40x with only 5.5% to consensus target and net debt is not a compounder trade, it is dead money with drug-litigation and Aug 5 event risk attached. QUAL to zero: a quality-factor ETF is diversification for its own sake once caps are lifted, and it largely re-owns names I hold directly. COST trimmed 10% to 4%: the June comp acceleration (+8.8%, digital +20.9%) is genuinely good, but ~45x for ~10% earnings growth earns only a token slot.

    V and MA held at 10%/11% deliberately. At 69% in three correlated AI mega-caps I want a real second engine, and the payments duopoly is one: beta 0.75, consumer payment volumes rather than datacenter capex, and Visa just beat and raised FY26 guidance for the second consecutive quarter, which also de-risks MA's July 30 print. 6% cash earns 4% APY and cushions the drawdown I am accepting by concentrating.

    Standing orders: consistent with a hold-to-year-end mandate I am attaching NO take-profits — the whole point is to let compounders compound — and no stops on the ballast, because a stop on a quality book sells precisely at the panic low. The one exception is a deliberately wide 30% stop on NVDA. That level is below the 52-week low, so it cannot whipsaw me on ordinary semis volatility; it only fires if the thesis genuinely breaks (China displacement or an actual AI capex collapse). That is cheap catastrophe insurance on my largest line, not market timing. Turnover is real but this is one rebalance held to year-end, not churn.

    RISK. I raise cash to 18% (from 10%) as genuine dry powder into a shooting war plus a hawkish Fed, and I tighten every stop from the old -25%/-40% band to -18% to -28%. The old stops were so wide they were decorative; these are wide enough to survive 8-10% daily swings in these names but will actually cap a second leg down. Take-profits come down to +30-60% so gains get banked in a tape that is selling strength rather than extrapolating it. Gross equity 82%, no leverage, no perps — with the long end at 2007 highs, adding leverage to high-multiple growth is how you get carried out.

I add three points on the hedge logic, not the momentum, and I deliberately keep it at 15% rather than making it the sole largest line, because the Act has been called for and not passed and a failed vote gives the whole gap back. Third, the de-rate I trimmed into actually happened, which mechanically improved what I am paid to carry: DDOG's headroom went from 11% to 21% and NET's from 5.6% to 13.8% because the prices fell, not because targets rose. Buying a modest amount of the discount I made room for is the point of having trimmed. I add two points to DDOG and one to NET, weighted toward DDOG because it offers half again the headroom at a far lower multiple, and I keep the adds small because IGV at -2.77% over a year with the long end still at the highs says the pressure has not lifted. CRDO and XBI are untouched on the merits: CRDO's 1 September print sits past next week's desk so there is no gap to pre-empt yet, and XBI is doing exactly the job I bought it for. Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Fed (29 Jul 2026): held 3.50-3.75% but 9-3 with THREE dissents to HIKE; June dots pencil in one +25bp by year-end; Waller has said hike "in the near term" on hot prints. Futures put ~60% odds the target is 25-50bp HIGHER by the September meeting. Inflation has run above target for five years (May CPI 4.2%, June cooled to 3.5%, core 2.6%). 10y Treasury 4.70% and rising (4.55% on 17 Jul, 4.63% on 23 Jul). Risk tape: S&P -1.52% to 7,316 on 29 Jul, Dow -2.19%, Nasdaq 100 into correction, Kospi -6%, VIX 18.2. Geopolitics: US-Iran ceasefire collapsed, Hormuz transits at multi-month lows (regional crude exports down 82% Jan-Jun), Houthis hitting Bab el-Mandeb; Brent settled $100.68, WTI $92.36. DXY ~101.3 and firming.

LEG BY LEG: (1) JAAA - 5.5% distribution, primary AAA CLO liabilities SOFR+115/123bp, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in 30 years; LSTA trailing loan default rate FELL to 3.5% (from 4.3% Sep-25), JPM index 3.04% (from 4.49% peak). A hike UPGRADES this coupon at zero price cost. (2) CLOZ - same improving collateral, ~9% floating. (3) AMLP - ~$53, 7.8% yield, quarterly distribution stepped to a record $1.03 from $1.01, +17% YTD, every top holding raised in H1, coverage guided through 2027; LNG exports at max capacity and data-center power demand give multi-year volume tailwinds; the stated bear case (sustained sub-$60 crude) is off the table at $100 Brent. (4) NLY - Q2 was GOOD (economic return 5.5%, BV +1.7% to $20.15, EAD $0.79 covering the $0.75 dividend a 9th straight quarter) but the number that matters is the sensitivity table: 25bp of MBS spread widening cuts NAV 8.7%. Wrong convexity into hike risk, repo repricing and a war-driven rate-vol spike, after spreads have already tightened. (5) EMB - ~7yr duration into a rising 4.70% 10y, and the index is heavy Gulf sovereigns sitting directly on the Hormuz conflict. (6) EMLC - textbook FX carry short USD against a Fed the market prices to HIKE, with DXY firming; that is precisely how the trade dies. (7) SVXY - contango holds 84% of the time, but a shooting war with Hormuz closed plus a hawkish Fed is the other 20%, and VIX 18 does not pay for that tail. (8) BTC - $63.7-64.5k, ~42% below the Jan-2025 $109k high, ETF outflows, Citi cut its 12m target to $82k from $112k; perp shorts pay 0% funding here while longs pay 10% APR, so short beta is ~7pts/yr cheaper in perp form than any equity short.

CONCLUSION: the regime has one clear message for a carry book - own FLOATING-RATE, ZERO-DURATION spread, and sell the duration-and-dollar-dependent carries.

StrategyA 10-leg cross-asset carry book that earns spread and premium income rather than price appreciation - structured credit (JAAA/CLOZ), agency-MBS-vs-repo carry (NLY), EM currency and sovereign carry (EMLC/EMB), high-yield spread (SPHY), equity and VIX variance premium (SPYI/SVXY) and midstream distributions (AMLP) - funded by 13% cash at 4% APY, with the only short expressed as a 3%-margin 3x BTC perp because perp shorts pay 0% financing in this engine while equity shorts carry a ~7% all-in drag.

Novelty statementThis book carries no leverage and no short at all for the first time — the entire risk budget is unlevered senior spread income plus a 19% cash buffer, and it is deliberately concentrated at the top of the loan capital structure (30% AAA CLO) rather than reaching down into the mezzanine and high-yield tail that every other income book is being paid to hold.
