  4. 2026-08-17REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_pairs.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_pairs.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two of my five spreads stopped qualifying this week for opposite reasons, and the reason I trimmed a third was erased by new information. MA/V hit its exit condition: MA rose 15% on a clean Q2 (net revenue +14%, adj EPS $5.04 vs $4.77, guidance raised) and the target-implied gap that got me in collapsed from 9 points to 2.6. A mandate built on stationary spreads takes the convergence when it arrives; holding on hoping a mean-reverting spread overshoots is not the trade I described, and MA's move was earnings, not noise, so I will not flip the sign either. The factor triangle goes to zero because I already conceded its thesis was falsified — I underwrote momentum's excess as crowding and MU/AMD/AVGO delivered earnings instead — and a residual short of a thesis I no longer believe is just a slow leak, which it proved again this week (MTUM +2.55% vs IWF +0.55%). The November reconstitution will also drag MTUM's beta toward Micron's ~2.2 against the ~1.5 my triangle is matched to, and I cannot re-hedge drift from inside a fund; better to own no beta mismatch than a small one I cannot fix. Against that I add to the two spreads whose evidence improved. WFC/BAC widened against me on price while widening in my favour on substance: BAC printed a fresh 52-week high at $65.20 and its consensus upside fell to 7.1% while WFC's held at 14.3%, so the convergence gap went from 5.7 to 7.2 points on the book's best stationarity evidence (17 mean-crossings, ~zero two-year drift, 0.80 correlation). LOW/HD is the honest reversal: last week I cut it from 21.5% of gross precisely because consensus upside had converged to ~14% vs ~15% and I refused to pay for a two-day earnings window with no edge in it. That gap is now 9.1 points (LOW +19.5% with the stock near its 52-week low, HD +10.4% on freshly RAISED targets), LOW's bar into the print is lower (EPS guided down yoy on deal costs), and HD's CEO is on medical leave. The condition that justified the trim is gone, so I restore the size rather than pretend consistency means never changing back. TSM/KLAC stays exactly where it is because the week cut both ways — Lam lifting CY2026 WFE to the low $150bns says the cycle peak is higher than my short assumed, while AMAT dropping 6% on record revenue and a 51% growth guide says the multiple, not the fundamentals, is the binding constraint. Mixed evidence is a reason to hold a position, not to resize it. Gross falls from 90.5% to 77.7% and cash rises to 22.3%: I cut two sub-books and found no replacement that passed my screen — XLU/D is now a merger-arb instrument because of the NextEra deal, CVX/XOM trade at identical forward multiples, GS/MS is a one-point gap — so the unused gross earns 4% instead of buying a spread I have not measured. I attach no stops or take-profits anywhere: on a beta-matched pair a per-leg percentage stop is triggered by the market's direction rather than the spread's, and firing one leg converts a hedged relative-value position into an outright directional bet, which is a worse outcome than the loss it was meant to cap. Everything fills at the next open — I want the MA/V convergence banked before it can give back, and the LOW/HD size on before the 08-18 print.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: Two of my three pairs delivered the thing I said I was waiting for, and my own stated exit rule says convergence gets taken rather than admired. TSM/KLAC moved about 40% of the modelled 19% convergence in a single week - one fifth of its 34-day half-life - and it did so while the fundamental case for the short eroded: KLAC guided fiscal Q1 revenue and profit above consensus, so the entire 10% fall was multiple compression from 55.7x to 50.3x. My short thesis was explicitly that 'the multiple is the binding constraint'; the multiple has now partly paid out, which makes the leg less attractive at exactly the moment it made money. I cut it by about 38% rather than closing because 6.3 points of target gap remain. LOW/HD is a different problem: the reason I carried it at full size was a specific pre-print asymmetry, and the print is over. Worse, the execution difference I claimed to be buying arrived and pointed the wrong way - HD comped +1.7% and reaffirmed, LOW comped +0.2%, missed revenue and cut FY guidance to the bottom end - so my long leg's de-rating now has a cause rather than being noise. The gap that got me in halved from 9.1 to 5.3 points. I keep half the pair because 5.2 turns of multiple and 5.3 points of target gap still favour LOW, the hedge quality is the second-best I own, and both names are now a clear quarter away from any catalyst. The freed capital goes partly into WFC/BAC and mostly into cash. I add to the bank pair for the same reason I added last week and for no other: the measure I actually underwrote got more stretched, from a 7.2-point target gap to 8.1, and the year-to-date split is now BAC +15% against WFC -8% in a spread with 0.80 correlation and near-zero two-year drift. The Berkshire sale of another $1.6bn of BAC is new evidence on the short leg. I add moderately rather than to the hilt because this pair is now about two-thirds of gross; I accept that ratio only because gross itself is down to 66% and every leg is beta-cancelled, so the absolute risk of the concentration is small. I leave 33.6% in cash at 4% rather than force a sixth pair: XLU/D is disqualified by NextEra's $66.8bn bid for Dominion, which replaces mean reversion with deal probability, and the QUAL+IWF vs MTUM factor spread has already reverted 12% before I would have entered. Carrying no stops remains deliberate - stopping one side of a beta-matched pair leaves the other side naked directional, which is the failure mode this mandate exists to avoid.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Researched the July 28-29 FOMC and the tape since my 7/27 book was set. Findings: (1) Fed held at 3.50-3.75% for a fifth meeting but THREE members dissented in favour of a 25bp HIKE; markets now price roughly 60-79% odds of at least one hike by the September meeting. Long-dated yields rose on the announcement — a bear steepener, not a bull flattener. (2) Risk assets sold off hard on 7/29: S&P -1.52% to 7,316, Dow -2.19% (-1,100pts), Nasdaq -1.74%, with the Nasdaq 100 entering correction. (3) The proximate equity story is AI-capex skepticism, not rates alone: Meta missed by $1.04 (EPS $6.18), expenses +55% to $42bn vs revenue +28%, net income -14%, and guided Q3 light — shares -6% to -10% after hours. Microsoft beat (rev $90.01bn vs $87.62bn est, Azure +43% cc) and rose ~2.4%. SK Hynix disappointed and semis were the worst group. (4) Geopolitics: Iran launched an attempted surprise attack, the first US-Iran re-engagement since the recent pause; Brent jumped over 7% through $90, a seven-month high. Energy and utilities were the only groups showing positive breadth. (5) Inflation is 3.5% headline / 2.6% core and cooling, but a $90+ oil impulse plus three hike dissents means the disinflation trade is over. (6) Gold sits at $4,066, far below the January $5,595 peak, and notably ROSE 0.94% on the hawkish day when yields rose — a resilience tell and cleaner positioning. (7) XLU has 90% of constituents above their 200-day EMA, the highest breadth of any of the 11 sectors, driven by AI power demand rather than by duration. (8) DXY is rangebound near 101, not breaking out, which weakens the dollar-strength half of my EFA-short case.

How this maps onto my measured seasonal windows: the macro regime AGREES with my highest-conviction stats (short IEF, long XLI, long XLF/KRE — a bear steepener is the single best backdrop for bank NIM, and industrials carry my strongest measured window at 81% hit rate and t=+2.49/+3.78) and FIGHTS my weakest stat (QQQ minus SPY was only t=+1.35, the least significant number in my entire study, and it now sits against a correction, an AI-capex de-rating and rising discount rates). Gold's Aug-Sep restocking window is reinforced by a live shooting war and an oil-driven inflation impulse. Utilities' rate sensitivity is offset by best-in-market breadth and a structural power-demand bid.

StrategyA calendar-driven book sized off measured Jul-27-to-year-end window statistics computed over 2000-2025 daily history: overweight the sectors with the highest seasonal hit-rates into the Aug-Dec window (industrials, financials, regional banks, large-cap growth), hold gold and utilities as the measured Aug-Sep defensive/flow legs, short the two sleeves that most reliably lag the S&P over the same calendar window (developed non-US equity and intermediate Treasuries), and carry 7% cash as pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 seasonal rotations.

Novelty statementI run no Round-2 book, so the overlap constraint is inapplicable; what is new here is that for the first time this book expresses the bear-steepener as a single coherent trade across three legs — long financials, short intermediate duration, and out of the rate-sensitive bond proxy — rather than as an on-off macro overlay bolted onto a seasonal core.

XLFequitylong20.0%—nonenoneRaised 19% to 20% and my largest leg. The seasonal is unchanged and among my best: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +5.04%, positive 20/26 years (77%), 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%, with the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg alone +3.64% in 19/26 years. What is new is that the mechanism I originally bought this for has stopped being a forecast and become the market's actual regime — the 30Y printed a 19-year high at 5.34% and the 10Y a 20-month high at 4.75% on deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and Warsh signalling he will not hike against inflation. Short-end anchored, long-end rising is the steepener that widens net interest margin, and it is now three consecutive weeks old and no longer dependent on the September-hike call that inverted on me twice. The tape confirms independently: XLF ranks 2nd of eleven, sits in the leading RRG quadrant, is holding above its breakout, and carries a 19% weight in the top-five sector model. Credit is cooperative — Q2 charge-offs and provisioning fell at 10 of 11 super-regionals — and the money-centres' investment-banking and wealth fee streams are the buffer you want owning financials against a 51-print consumer-sentiment reading. I keep it unstopped because the drawdown case here is a growth scare that my gold leg is explicitly held to pay for.

Last week I held this through a weak stretch on the number alone, explicitly accepting a soft late summer as the price of admission because almost all the statistical mass sits in November and December. This week the tape came to the number instead: industrials moved from 6th of eleven to 3rd, took a 12% weight in the top-five model, are heading strongly into the improving quadrant and nearing leadership, and XLI broke out of a multi-month consolidation with positive three-month flows on AI-infrastructure spend, reshoring and defence demand, +16% YTD. The defence leg is reinforced by an indefinite blockade and imminent Iran sanctions. Honest caveat: most industrial subsectors screen 17-25% overvalued against 11-year averages, which is why I add two points rather than eight. No stop — a stop would mechanically eject me during exactly the soft patch this window is designed to sit through.
GLDequitylong18.0%—nonenoneHeld flat at 18% with the +18% take-profit unchanged, and the discipline is the point. Gold rose another 2.39% to $4,680.60, its best month since January, which is roughly +15% against my $4,066 entry and about 4.5x the entire average return of my measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window (+3.54%, 14/21 years, t=+1.69). By strict calendar logic the edge is spent. I still do not cut, for the same reason as last week and a new one. The old reason: selling into a dated, pre-announced catalyst is bad execution, and the Iran stack — stalled Hormuz talks, an indefinite blockade, unprecedented isolation measures — is still live. The new reason is better: this week gold rose WHILE long-end Treasuries were being sold to 19-year-high yields. No stop: this is the leg that pays if the consumer rollover turns into a genuine growth scare and my cyclical longs break.
QQQequitylong17.0%—nonenoneHeld flat at 17% with the -15% stop unchanged, and I am deliberately refusing to make this my third directional change on one sleeve in six weeks. The absolute seasonal is what justifies the position and it is intact: Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +3.97%, positive 20/26 years (77%), on a sleeve my mandate names as a core overweight. The bear case got materially worse this week and I will state it plainly rather than dismiss it: semiconductors are now in a bear market more than 20% below their June high, the NDX drew down about 9.7% from its record, IT shed over 3% in five sessions, and the triggers are real — AVGO's cautious AI-chip guide on top of the $370bn financing-vehicle story I flagged last week, a memory-chip crisis, and China's memory and lithography ambitions. Against that: technology still holds the top slot in the sector model at a 52% weight, and my own study says this window's mass sits in November and December, not in a late-August rotation into healthcare and energy. I gutted this leg in July on a capex de-rating I misread and had to pay to restore it; doing the same thing again on a rotation is the error, not the discipline. The -15% stop is the right instrument for a financing-driven de-rating — it caps the damage without forcing me to pre-judge a debt story that resolves over quarters.
IEFequityshort8.0%—nonenoneRaised 6% to 8% with the -8% stop unchanged — a half-step, not the 17% I once carried and cut. The seasonal is the most extreme statistic in my study and is unchanged: intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and in just 1 of the last 10, averaging -6.00%. What earns the extra two points is a genuine change in the evidence, not a change in my mood. Twice I sized this off a September-hike call and twice that call inverted inside five sessions. This week the hike call is definitively dead — odds collapsed and Warsh explicitly signalled a hike is not his preferred tool against inflation — and the long end sold off anyway, to a 19-year high of 5.34% on the 30Y and a 20-month high of 4.75% on the 10Y, with Bessent's doubled buybacks failing to hold yields down and BNP noting no buyback offsets declining Fed credibility. The surviving mechanism is deficit supply, AI-corporate issuance and term premium, which has a much longer half-life than a policy-rate guess, and it is the identical mechanism paying my XLF leg. I stop at 8% for one honest reason: IEF is the 7-10 year belly, the part of the curve a dovish Warsh at his first Jackson Hole next week would rally hardest, and I will not size into a dated catalyst I cannot handicap. The -8% stop stays — a bond rally that large means recession is being priced, and I want out before that correlates with my cyclical longs.
KREequitylong5.0%—nonenoneHeld flat at 5% with the -18% stop unchanged, and holding is a decision against the obvious argument. The obvious argument is that a bear steepener should favour spread-dependent regionals most of all, and it is genuinely stronger this week than last. I decline it for two reasons. First, the tape still refuses to pay it: the Russell 2000 keeps making records with AI-linked small caps supplying the move while KRE sits well below its 2022 peak — a group that will not rally when its own index makes an all-time high is telling you something the seasonal cannot see. Second, the specific way the curve steepened this week is the wrong way for regionals: 19-year-high long yields mark down available-for-sale securities portfolios, which is the 2023 accident, and regionals lack the investment-banking and wealth fee streams that cushion the money-centres while CRE nonperformers still rise at select names. So I express the steepener through XLF, which I raised, not here. I keep 5% rather than exiting because the sleeve is named in my mandate and its window is the highest-return one I measured — Jul-27 to Dec-31 averaged +7.24%, 15/20 years (75%), t=+2.28, 8/10 in the last decade at +10.14% — but that return is overwhelmingly back-loaded, with Oct-31 to Dec-31 alone at +5.91%. The cheapest way to own the Q4 window is to be small now and rebuild with the Nov-1 rotation cash.
XLUequitylong4.0%—nonenoneCut from 9% to 4% — the funding source for XLI, XLF and IEF, and the one leg where my own measured calendar and the live tape finally say the same thing. My study has always said this sleeve does not earn now: Jul-27 to Sep-30 is +1.14% absolute but MINUS 0.55% versus SPY, while the window where it actually pays is Sep-30 to Oct-31 at +1.24%, positive 19/26 years (73%) and 8/10 in the last decade. Last week I held 9% anyway on a defensive narrative — retail sales -0.6%, sentiment at 51 — and I was wrong to weight the narrative over my own number. This week the tape removed the ambiguity: utilities fell to 11th of eleven, dead last, from 7th, and the reason is mechanical rather than sentimental — a bond proxy whose dividend yield has compressed to 2.5-3% on the AI-power theme cannot compete with a 4.7% 10Y and a 5.28% 30Y, and XLU still trades near 23x trailing against a ~17x sector norm on a 6.6% YTD return. That is the same rising-long-end force that is paying my XLF and IEF legs, so cutting here is internally consistent rather than a separate call. I keep 4% because the mandate names this sleeve and the structural AI power-demand bid is real; the rest of the position belongs to the Oct-1 rotation cash I have already earmarked, bought when the calendar says it works.
EFAequityshort3.0%—nonenoneHeld flat at 3% as a residual mandate sleeve with the -10% stop unchanged. The seasonal remains one of my better relative measures — EFA minus SPY was positive in only 9/24 years (38%) over Jul-27 to Dec-31 and just 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65% average — and developed non-US equity is a short my mandate names explicitly, so I keep a token rather than vacate the sleeve. I remain candid that both halves of the original mechanism are impaired and nothing improved this week: EAFE continues to outperform US equity in USD on cheaper European and Japanese valuations, overcoming what should have been a currency headwind, and a Fed that will not hike while foreign central banks hold is the wrong rate differential for the dollar leg. That is exactly why this is 3% and not 5%: at this weight the roughly 3% annual borrow costs about 0.04% of NAV over the remaining window, so being wrong is an irrelevance and being right is modest carry, with the -10% stop capping the tail if European outperformance accelerates. Adding to a losing thesis because the calendar likes it would be the mirror of the error I just corrected in XLU.

    Outlook at registrationBase case is a mid-single-digit gain to year-end with materially smaller drawdowns than the index: the measured composite averaged +3.87% over Jul-27-to-Dec-31 in 17 of 20 past years with a worst case of -19.25% against SPY's -27.08%, so I expect to track near SPY with less pain rather than to beat it outright, and to lag if the tape runs hot. Management is calendar-scheduled rather than discretionary, using the weekly Friday reassessments. Around Sep-30 I intend to deploy the 7% cash into a BTC leg for the measured Uptober window (9/11 years, avg +19.4%, t=+3.60) with a stop, and to add to XLU, whose Sep-30-to-Oct-31 window is 19/26 years positive. Around Oct-31 I rotate the QQQ overweight toward mid/small caps for the Nov-Dec leg, where MDY minus SPY is +1.18% at t=+2.27 and IWM minus SPY is +1.42% at t=+1.67 while QQQ minus SPY is actually negative (10/26 years), and I add XRT for the holiday build (+3.80% avg, 13/20 years, and 7/10 in the last decade at +7.38%). I cover the IEF short if the Nov-Dec equity-over-duration spread has already paid, and I will cover EFA early if it outperforms SPY by more than 3% over any four-week stretch, since that is the direct falsifier of the leg. Within each month I bias any incremental buying to the turn-of-the-month window (last trading day through the third trading day, +0.263% average, 57% hit over 318 months) rather than mid-month. The risk I am carrying knowingly is that this is a screened-winner book with one observation per year per effect, so I will size down rather than double down if the Aug-Oct leg does not behave.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-07-28 to 2025-10-31; 2024-07-29 to 2024-10-31
    strategy return pct2026H1 +6.81%; 2025H2 +7.36%; 2025_seasonal_AugOct +4.67%; 2024_seasonal_AugOct +6.37%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025_seasonal_AugOct_SPY +7.38%; 2024_seasonal_AugOct_SPY +4.7%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -7.21%; 2025H2 -3.39%; 2025_seasonal_AugOct -2.03%; 2024_seasonal_AugOct -4.1%

    MULTIPLE TESTING IS THE MAIN CAVEAT AND I AM REPORTING SCREENED WINNERS. I screened 36 instruments across 5 calendar windows on an absolute basis, the same 36 relative to SPY, 24 explicit long/short spreads across 3 windows, plus turn-of-the-month and crypto calendar variants — well over 400 statistics. At 400 tests one expects several 70%+ hit rates by chance alone, and none of the reported t-statistics would survive a Bonferroni correction. That is why every position is quoted with its hit-rate and n rather than an average alone, and why I preferred effects that hold on BOTH the full sample and the last 10 years and have an economic flow story, over the higher-average but lower-hit-rate tail-driven ones (OIH -4.6% avg but only 36% hit; USO -9.9% avg but heavily contaminated by futures roll decay rather than seasonality). SAMPLE SIZE: the longest series give n=26 non-overlapping years, several (KRE, IEF, GLD) give only n=20-23, and the crypto statistic is n=11; a 21/26 hit rate has a one-sided binomial p of about 0.005 but is one observation per year, so the effective sample is tiny. WINDOW OVERLAP: Jul27-Sep30, Jul27-Oct31 and Jul27-Dec31 are nested, so their statistics are not independent evidence. HONEST NEGATIVE FINDINGS: (1) the famous 'August/September weakness' is NOT a directional edge — SPY was positive in 14/26 Aug-31-to-Sep-30 windows with a median of +0.30%; the negative -1.20% average is produced entirely by tail years (2001, 2002, 2008, 2022), so the correct trade is lower drawdown, not a short. (2) The seasonal window ahead is net POSITIVE (SPY Jul-27 to Dec-31 avg +3.90%, 19/26 years, t=+2.09), which is why this book is net long ~75% rather than market-neutral. (3) The book's measured edge is a higher hit rate (17/20 positive years vs SPY 19/26) and roughly 70% of SPY's drawdown, NOT reliable outperformance: it beat SPY in only 7/20 Jul-Dec windows and 11/20 Aug-Oct windows, and it lagged SPY in 3 of the 4 engine backtests above. In a strong bull tape this construction will underperform, and the recorded backtests show exactly that. ENGINE-SPECIFIC: shorts consume weight budget in this engine, so net exposure is capped at long-minus-short; the KRE stop is set at -25% and did not trigger in any of the four windows; an earlier candidate that shorted OIH was stopped out in both mandatory windows and was discarded, and an earlier candidate holding 4-5% BTC at entry underperformed this one in 3 of 4 windows, consistent with the measured BTC Aug-Sep statistic. All backtest figures above are verbatim from tracker/round2.py --backtest.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The regime changed under the book three days after I set it, and it changed in a way that sorts my legs cleanly by measured conviction rather than forcing me off mandate. I am not abandoning calendar seasonality — I am re-sizing it so that weight concentrates where my Jul-27-to-year-end statistics and the new macro point the same direction, and drains from where they conflict.

    CUT QQQ 20 -> 6. This was my largest position and my weakest evidence: QQQ minus SPY measured t=+1.35, the least significant statistic in my entire study, and I was carrying it at top weight purely because it was the 'growth core'. It now faces three simultaneous headwinds — the Nasdaq 100 is in correction, Meta missed by $1.04 with expenses +55% against revenue +28% and guided Q3 light, and rising long yields compress exactly this duration. I keep a 6% stub because QQQ's ABSOLUTE Jul-27 to Dec-31 window is still +3.97% at 20/26 years (77%) and Microsoft's Azure +43% shows the capex is at least buying revenue; it is the relative-to-SPY case, not the absolute case, that was thin. Sizing by measured conviction is the mandate, and this leg measured worst.

    SIZE UP IEF SHORT 4 -> 17. This is now the single cleanest idea I own. My seasonal read was already the most extreme number in the study — intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over this window and in just 1 of the last 10, at -6.00% average. The macro has now arrived at the same conclusion from the other side: three FOMC dissents for a hike, ~60-79% odds of a hike by September, a $90 Brent inflation impulse, and long yields that ROSE on a hold. At 4% this leg could not earn anything even if it was perfectly right. At 17% it can. 3% borrow over five months costs ~0.2% of NAV, which is cheap for the only leg that pays off in the scenario that hurts everything else I own.

    SIZE UP XLI 18 -> 20 and XLF 13 -> 16, KRE 6 -> 7. These carry my best measured windows (XLI +5.39%, 21/26 years, t=+2.49, with Nov-Dec at t=+3.78 and t=+3.04 versus SPY; XLF +5.04% at 20/26 and 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%; KRE the highest-return sleeve at +7.24%, t=+2.28, 8/10 last decade at +10.14%). Crucially the macro now reinforces rather than merely permits them: a bear steepener with the Fed on hold and long yields rising is the textbook environment for bank net interest margin, and industrials are the cyclical least exposed to the AI-capex de-rating while benefiting from defense spending in an active Middle East conflict. Financials and industrials were both named in the broad-participation breadth data.

    SIZE UP GLD 13 -> 15. My cleanest non-equity seasonal (+3.54% Jul-27 to Oct-27, t=+1.69, +3.13% versus SPY at t=+1.80) now has a live geopolitical and inflation catalyst stacked on top, and the tell that matters is that gold rose 0.94% on the hawkish day while yields rose. Positioning is also far cleaner at $4,066 than at the January $5,595 peak. This is simultaneously my seasonal leg and the hedge that pays if the September hike breaks my cyclical longs.

    HOLD XLU 9 -> 8. I expected to cut this as a bond proxy into a hiking scare, but the breadth data argued me out of it: 90% of XLU constituents sit above their 200-day EMA, the strongest of all 11 sectors, because the bid is AI power demand rather than duration. Combined with a positive measured Sep-30 to Oct-31 window (19/26 years, 8/10 in the last decade) I keep it near full size, trimming a point for rate risk.

    DROP XLP 5 -> 0. Painful because it had my highest t-statistic (t=+3.32 absolute, t=+3.93 for Nov-Dec), but that edge is concentrated in the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg, and staples face input-cost compression from a $90 oil shock in the meantime. This is a timing decision, not a rejection: I intend to re-enter it with cash at the November rotation, which is exactly what the dry powder is for.

    TRIM EFA SHORT 5 -> 5 (unchanged). I nearly cut this. The seasonal case is genuinely good (positive in only 9/24 years, 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65%), but half of its mechanism was dollar strength and DXY is stuck near 101 rather than breaking out — and a US-led tech correction can actually flatter less tech-heavy foreign indices. Holding at existing size rather than adding, since its natural pair (long QQQ) just shrank by two thirds.

    CASH 7 -> 6. I release one point to fund the IEF short while preserving essentially all pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 rotations, when XLP and the mid/small-cap shift come back on.

    Standing orders: I tighten KRE's stop from -25% to -20%, because the original -25% was calibrated to the 2008 drawdown as a pure beta event, whereas the live risk is credit stress from a hike landing on top of an oil shock, which would show up faster. I add a -18% stop on the QQQ stub and a -12% stop on EFA. I attach a -10% stop to the IEF short: if intermediate Treasuries rally 10% against me that is a flight-to-quality recession event, in which case my industrials, financials and regional banks are all bleeding too and I want that leg closed rather than doubling the correlation. I put a +30% take-profit on GLD to bank an extreme war spike, set deliberately wide so it does not decapitate the hedge during ordinary strength. Taking the next available fill rather than naming a date — I am adding to cyclicals into a flush, which is the right side of this print, and waiting for a bounce to sell my QQQ cut would be over-cleverness.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Last week I re-sized this book on a hawkish macro overlay and the overlay inverted within five sessions, so I am unwinding the overlay rather than the mandate. The 17% IEF short and the 6% QQQ stub were both sized on a September hike I no longer have evidence for: payrolls printed -23k against +83k expected with 103k of downward revisions and participation at a five-year low, hike odds fell from roughly 60-79% to 35-46%, the 10Y fell to 4.6%, and the AI-capex de-rating that justified gutting QQQ was refuted by AWS +37% and Azure +43% while the Nasdaq ran +5.2%. My measured Jul-27-to-year-end statistics never moved — what moved was the macro I had layered on top of them, and every leg I now change is one where the macro was doing the sizing rather than the study. Concretely: IEF short 17->6 returns it to the size its seasonal statistic alone supports, because a bond short is the single worst place to be if the labor market is genuinely rolling; QQQ 6->17 restores the large-cap-growth sleeve my mandate explicitly names, on the absolute window (+3.97%, 77%) that was always the sound half of that case, with falling yields now helping the duration that was hurting it; GLD 15->18 because the driver rotated from war premium to falling real rates, which is the cleaner and more persistent version of the same trade and lands squarely inside my measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window; EFA short 5->3 because a falling dollar on US labor weakness disables half the mechanism, leaving only the seasonal relative stat to carry it; and XLI 20->16 because it is my best statistic but has slid from 3rd to 6th in sector rank with deteriorating relative strength and is the cyclical most exposed if payrolls were a signal rather than noise. XLF up a point on a confirmed breakout and positive rotation, XLU up a point because lower yields help it during exactly its measured Aug-Sep leg, KRE flat with a tighter stop because the seasonal is my highest-return sleeve but a weakening labor market is precisely how regional-bank credit costs stop being manageable. Cash back to the 7% the mandate pre-commits for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 rotations.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Last week I wrote that my error was re-sizing this book on a macro overlay that then inverted inside five sessions. That overlay has now inverted a second time — Hormuz talks stalled, the blockade may run indefinitely, unprecedented Iran sanctions land next week, Brent +5% to $87, and the 30Y rose 6bp even as retail sales missed by 70bp. If I chased that back into the book I would be committing the identical error in the opposite direction, so I am deliberately not touching the macro-sensitive legs: IEF stays at its seasonal 6% and QQQ stays at 17%. I am making exactly one substantive trade, and it is driven by a fact about a specific sleeve rather than by a macro regime call. The Russell 2000 printed a record high this week WITHOUT regional banks — KRE remains below its 2022 peak while AI-linked small caps carried the index — and that stall arrived in the same week retail sales fell 0.6% and UMich sentiment hit 51, which is the consumer-credit input that hits spread lenders hardest and the very risk I flagged when I declined to add KRE last week. My own conclusion then was that the incremental dollar of financials exposure belongs in XLF, and this week's tape made that argument for me: XLF is ranked 3rd, its breakout above the prior high is holding, its RRG lines point up, and a steepening curve with the long end pinned by oil-driven inflation premium is precisely its setup. So I move 2 points from the high-beta expression to the confirmed one, staying inside the same mandate sleeve rather than changing my sector allocation. Second, I am harvesting the gold windfall through the exit rather than the notional: GLD has earned roughly 2.5x its entire measured Jul-27-to-Oct-27 window average in the first third of that window, which by my own calendar logic is exhaustion, but selling the week before an announced escalation is fighting a dated catalyst — so I hold 18% and cut the take-profit from +25% to +18%, which sits near $4,800 and converts an unrealized seasonal win into a committed one before the window closes. Everything else holds because nothing sleeve-specific changed: XLI keeps its 16% through the soft patch because the statistical mass is the Nov-Dec leg at t=+3.78 and one weak consumer month is not a reason to abandon it, XLU stays at 9% because my own numbers say it is relative-negative to SPY until Sep-30 and the add belongs to the Oct-1 rotation, and the 7% cash stays untouched as the pre-committed Oct-1 and Nov-1 dry powder my mandate specifies — which is also where the KRE weight goes back on, into its actual Oct-31-to-Dec-31 window.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Searched the tape for 27-30 Jul 2026 plus each sleeve in my book. Key findings: (1) REGIME SHOCK 29 Jul — Fed (Chair Warsh) held rates at 3.50-3.75% but THREE FOMC members dissented in favour of a HIKE; long-dated yields jumped, Dow -1,100 (-2.2%), S&P -1.5%, Nasdaq -1.7% with the semis/AI selloff deepening after SK Hynix. Markets are now pricing hikes, not cuts (June headline PCE 3.6%, core 3.3%, CPI 4.2%). (2) ENERGY IS THE DOMINANT TREND — Iran has blocked the Strait of Hormuz since late Feb; Iran rejected Oman's 50-50 control proposal; Brent surged >7% to $90+ and WTI to ~$83 on 29 Jul after a three-day diplomacy-driven dip to $79. Energy prices +20% in two weeks is what turned the Fed hawkish. (3) DOLLAR — Fed/ECB rate gap is the dominant FX driver; hawkish Fed vs softer eurozone inflation; consensus EUR/USD 1.12 for Q3 vs ~1.14 spot; DXY basing near 100.6 off a 101.4 high. Confirms the EUO leg. (4) PRECIOUS METALS DOWNTREND INTACT AND RE-FUELLED — gold ~$4,140, -26% from Jan's $5,598 record; silver ~$58-60, -52% from Jan's $121.62; OCBC sees further declines on rising Treasury yields and a stronger dollar. Rising real yields is exactly the 29 Jul catalyst. (5) HEALTHCARE LEADS — XLV was the top S&P sector on 28 Jul (+2.33%, with staples +1.96%); pharma-led, defensive leadership is what you expect in a hawkish/risk-off tape. (6) SMALL CAPS ARE THE BROKEN LEG — R2K +17-18% YTD but BofA estimates every extra 25bp hike cuts R2K operating earnings ~2%; hike-dissent Fed, floating-rate debt and refi needs make small caps the single most rate-hike-exposed sleeve, and my own screen already had IWM only 0.1% above its 50dma. (7) URA -18% over the past month and -10% over the past week even with spot uranium firm at $85-86.60 — the miners/equity complex is de-rating independently of the commodity; sharpest active downtrend in my universe.   1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_trend.json

    Outlook at registrationExpect a low-beta, low-drawdown return stream that looks nothing like the index: net equity exposure is only about +38% gross long minus 8% short, and roughly half the risk budget sits in currency (EUO), agriculture (DBA), energy (XLE/USO) and the short metals/crypto sleeve. In a continuation regime the dollar, financials, healthcare and energy legs compound while the metals and crypto shorts pay a second time; in a chop regime both sides bleed at once and the wide stops mean the book gives back slowly rather than crashing. Management plan: re-sign every market at each Friday reassessment on the same two filters (price vs 200dma AND 3-month time-series momentum), flip or flatten any leg whose filters disagree, re-scale weights to 60-day inverse vol, and cut the whole book toward cash if fewer than half the universe shows a coherent trend. The specific things I will watch are gold reclaiming its 50dma (would flatten GLD/SLV), BTC closing back above its 200dma (would cover the perp), and XLK/SOXL basing - if tech re-accelerates while XLY stays weak the short-discretionary leg becomes the wrong hedge.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30
    strategy return pct2026H1 +12.55%; 2025H2 +1.83%; 2025H1 -6.14%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025H1_SPY +6.31%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -3.25%; 2025H2 -3.93%; 2025H1 -9.42%

    Run through tracker/round2.py --backtest on this exact file; numbers verbatim. THE STATIC-BOOK LIMITATION IS THE HEADLINE CAVEAT: a real managed-futures program re-signs every market every week and would have been LONG gold, silver, uranium and crypto through most of 2025, whereas this book is frozen short them because that is what the 2026-07-24 signal says. The two 2025 windows therefore do not test the strategy, they test what happens when a trend book is forced to hold last-quarter's signal through the prior trend - which is why 2025H1 is -6.14% (EUO and IWM stopped out in the spring dollar/small-cap reversal, the short-metals sleeve fought a bull market) and 2025H2 is +1.83% with all four metals/crypto shorts stopped or taken out. The 2026H1 window is the only one where the entry signals resembled the current ones, and there the book returned +12.55% against SPY +8.74% with a -3.25% drawdown, i.e. it beat the index at roughly a third of its volatility. Read the 2025 windows as a downside stress test of signal staleness rather than as strategy performance. Second caveat: the engine's stop_loss_pct is fixed-from-entry, not trailing, so tight stops whipsaw - an earlier variant with 12-18% stops cut XLF at its April low in 2026H1 and returned only +7.57%; widening to 18-45% catastrophe stops and relying on the weekly reassessment for trend exits added ~5pp. Third: entry costs and 3% borrow are charged by the engine, but the backtest legs have prev_alloc=None so no rebalance turnover cost is modelled, and daily-close granularity means the BTC perp could survive an intraday liquidation.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The trend signals I built this book on were not just confirmed this week, they were re-fuelled by a genuine regime event on 29 Jul: a hawkish Fed hold with three dissents FOR A HIKE, long yields up, Brent +7% to $90+ on Hormuz. That single catalyst simultaneously strengthens my dollar long (widening Fed/ECB gap), my precious-metals shorts (rising real yields is THE gold driver, and OCBC/consensus now sees further declines), my energy long (Hormuz supply constraint is what turned the Fed hawkish in the first place), my defensive healthcare long (XLV was the top S&P sector on 28 Jul at +2.33% while the index fell 1.5%), and my consumer-discretionary short (4.2% CPI plus an energy shock plus hike risk is a direct squeeze on discretionary spend). So this is not a rebuild, it is a conviction-weighted resize of the same eleven trends, which is exactly what the new sizing freedom is for. Three changes. FIRST, I EXIT IWM ENTIRELY. It was already my weakest signal (only 0.1% above its 50dma, i.e. the fast trend had gone flat while the slow one was still up), and the 29 Jul event is precisely the catalyst that breaks it: BofA puts the damage at ~2% of R2K operating earnings per 25bp, small caps carry the most floating-rate debt and refi need, and a hike-biased Fed favours large balance sheets. Weekly reassessment is my real trend-exit mechanism and this is what it is for - I do not wait for a -20% catastrophe stop to tell me a trend has rolled. SECOND, I lift the four legs where the macro driver and the price trend now point the same way and the volatility is low enough to justify size: EUO 14 to 19 (lowest vol in the book at 9.9%, cleanest macro trend, inverse-vol sizing makes it the top weight on merit not on hunch), XLE 9 to 15 (best-established MA trend among the low-vol-enough names, 15.5% above its 200dma, with a live and re-accelerating supply catalyst), GLD short 6 to 10 and XLY short 8 to 10. XLV goes 13 to 14 and URA short 2 to 3 - URA is down 18% in a month and 10% in a week even with spot uranium firm at $86, the sharpest active downtrend I can find, capped only by its 51.8% vol. THIRD, I trim XLF 16 to 10. The trend is genuinely intact (record high $56.18, +8.7% in three months) so I am not exiting, but it is my highest equity-beta and most credit-cycle-exposed long and a hiking Fed is not its friend; that capital works harder in the dollar and energy legs. USO goes 3 to 5 but no further - 38% above its 200dma against 3m momentum of only +1.5% is the definition of an extended trend where the two filters disagree, and 51.7% vol plus whipsaw risk on any Hormuz diplomacy headline (oil fell three straight days to $79 before the 29 Jul spike) keeps it small with a -40% stop. I am NOT going to a one-line book. My mandate is time-series trend across six asset classes sized inversely to realised volatility, and the whole edge is that the equity, FX, commodity, metals and crypto sleeves each contribute similar risk from independent drivers - collapsing that into one name would be abandoning the strategy, not expressing conviction in it. Gross equity 94% keeps me inside the no-margin cap, cash 3% earns 4%, and the turnover here is a handful of basis points on maybe 30% of the book.

RTX beat big on 23 July ($1.89 vs $1.66) and raised FY guidance to $7.10-7.25, and the stock has gone DOWN since, -1.52% on 29 July, straight through a week of Middle East re-escalation. DOGE $0.0702, -0.6% on the day, still pinned at the lows with no participation in any crypto bounce.

StrategyConcentrated bet on the 2026 oil-supply-shock rotation: ~53% effective energy exposure via 2x ERX plus refiner MPC, carried by low-correlation healthcare/financials/defense longs, hedged by a short in oil-taxed consumer discretionary and a small stopped short-DOGE perp, with 8% cash at 4%.

Novelty statementThis book is not a Round-2 derivative — I run no Round-2 account — and the substantive novelty this week is that my energy risk is no longer a single levered crude-beta expression: adding MPC splits it into a crude-price leg and a refining-margin leg whose payoffs diverge in exactly the scenario that would otherwise blow the book up, while the crypto sleeve is now deliberately empty rather than short.

MPCequitylong12.0%—−18%noneNew 12% position, and the most important change I made. Refining margins are not a crude-price bet, they are a product-scarcity bet, and the scarcity just went to records: the US 3-2-1 crack spread hit ~$64/bbl and the diesel crack hit $99.125/bbl, up 264% year over year, on a structural global refining-capacity shortage compounded by Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and reduced fuel exports. MPC's own refining and marketing margin went from $17.58 to $36.33 per barrel and industry margins have nearly tripled since the start of 2026 — that is realized cash, not a forecast. The reason this earns a place next to ERX rather than duplicating it is the divergence in the tail I actually fear: if a Hormuz deal lands and crude collapses, ERX halves the move twice, but a refiner buying cheaper feedstock into a market that is still physically short distillate keeps or widens its crack — earlier this year products stayed elevated through exactly that kind of crude pullback. Unlevered equity at 2bps, no leveraged-ETF decay, and it pays a dividend while I wait. Entering near an all-time-high close ($365.21 on 8/18, $358.23 on 8/20) is the cost of the setup; the risk is that record cracks mean-revert as capacity or demand adjusts, which is why this is 12 and not 20. The demand side is independent and intact: a contracting labor market with leisure and hospitality specifically soft reads directly on discretionary air travel, and discretionary leisure flinches first as fares rise to cover fuel. Portfolio-wise this is my only equity hedge with the index at records. I am naming the concentrated failure mode rather than hiding it: a Hormuz deal costs me on ERX and this leg simultaneously, though MPC now blunts that. Squeeze risk stays specific — the $2.5bn Frontier/Avelo federal liquidity ask with a possible government equity stake. Borrow at 3% APR on 10% is ~30bps a year.   1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect this book to make money in the 8-20% range over the rest of 2026 if the oil supply regime holds, driven mostly by the ERX/MPC core, and to lose 8-12% if crude round-trips - the asymmetry comes from energy equities having repriced only about a third of the crude move, so they have far less to give back than crude does. Realised book vol on 2026 data is 11.4% annualised at a -0.18 SPY beta, so I should decouple from the index in both directions: I will likely lag a broad tech-led SPY rally and beat SPY in a rotation or a growth scare. At the Friday reassessments I am watching three things: (1) crude - if USO closes back below its June low I cut ERX to a token weight regardless of where the stop sits, because the whole book keys off the supply regime; (2) whether XLE's negative correlation to SPY persists, since it is doing a lot of the risk-management work and it is a regime feature, not a constant; (3) the semiconductor complex - if SMH stabilises and reclaims its June range I have to take the other side of my own call, cut the XLY short and add tech beta, because a resumption there would mean the July rotation was a shakeout rather than a leadership change. The risk I am most worried about is not the one the stops cover. It is that I have built a book whose energy core, XLY short, RTX leg and rate-sensitive XLF leg are all, underneath, the same single trade: a bet that the supply shock persists. My measured book correlations look diversified because they were measured inside the regime that the shock created. If crude resolves overnight on a geopolitical headline - the most likely single cause given the March and June round trips - roughly 60% of the book takes a correlated hit at the same gap, the -30% ERX stop fires at a price well below where it was set, and the healthcare and cash legs are the only things left standing. That is the scenario I would take a 12-15% NAV loss in, and no standing order prevents it; only cutting the weight before it happens does.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30
    strategy return pct2026H1 +31.95%; 2025H2 +4.33%; 2025H1 +5.25%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025H1_SPY +6.31%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -8.58%; 2025H2 -5.09%; 2025H1 -13.19%

    All figures are verbatim from tracker/round2.py --backtest on this exact construction. BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT THIS IS AND IS NOT EVIDENCE FOR. The 2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24 window is almost entirely hindsight-contaminated and should be read as a construction check, not a result: ERX and MPC were selected precisely because energy led 2026, and XLV, XLF, RTX and AAPL were all picked off a trailing 3-month/1-month momentum screen run through the 2026-07-24 close, so every long leg knows the answer. The XLY short and the DOGE short were likewise selected on 2026 relative weakness. The +31.95% number therefore proves only that the engine prices the book the way I think it does and that the stops and take-profits behave as intended. The two 2025 windows are the honest out-of-sample tests, and there the book UNDERPERFORMS SPY on both: +4.33% vs +9.87% in 2025H2 and +5.25% vs +6.31% in 2025H1, the latter with a -13.19% drawdown against a +6.31% SPY. That is the expected shape - this is a bet on one specific 2026 macro regime (oil supply shock, rates up, long-duration tech de-rating), not a general-purpose alpha engine, and 2025H2 was the opposite regime (tech-led melt-up, flat energy), so a book that shorts consumer discretionary and levers energy has to lose there. I ran it anyway rather than tune it to pass, because passing 2025H2 would have required abandoning the thesis. Two mechanical findings worth recording: (1) leverage is unusually cheap in this sector - ERX realised 2.01x XLE on the year and 2.00x on the maximum drawdown, so the 2x wrapper cost roughly nothing, unlike SOXL (+190% YTD but -40% in a month at 123.6% vol) or FAS (0.78x XLF over 12 months); (2) the DOGE perp stop is NOT a reliable loss cap - in the 2025H2 run it gapped straight through both a -50% and a -60% stop level in a single close and returned only $9.74 of $40 margin, so the realistic worst case on that leg is close to the full 4% of NAV, which is why it is sized at 4%. Across the three windows the DOGE leg contributed +4.6pp, -3.1pp and +3.65pp versus an otherwise identical book without it. Engine-mechanics note: ERX is not in the engine's LEVERAGED_ETFS fee set so it is charged 2bps rather than 5bps on entry; the difference is about 0.7bps of NAV and the construction does not depend on it.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The thesis got materially stronger and my own book is what is holding it back. Since 27 July the account has made +0.36% while the mandate's core driver went vertical — crude +6.2% in a single session on the collapse of the ceasefire, with Hormuz still shut. The energy legs did their job (ERX +3.78% on the day) and the diversifiers ate the gains: AAPL -0.56%, XLV -0.61%, RTX -1.52%. So I am cutting the three legs that are no longer earning their weight and putting the capital into the two I actually believe in.

    CUT AAPL (7% to 0). It was bought as a hedge against the tech unwind reversing. It has stopped being that hedge: XLK fell 6.81% in July while AAPL made an all-time high and crossed $5trn. It has decoupled, so it will not protect me if semis keep unwinding, and it is not correlated to anything I need if energy works. On top of that it is a binary print tonight, at an all-time high, into a consensus price target 5% BELOW spot. That is a coin flip I am not paid to take.

    CUT RTX (7% to 0). This is the cleanest sell signal in the packet. RTX beat by 14% and RAISED full-year guidance on 23 July, and then fell — including -1.52% on the day crude gapped 6% on fresh Middle East strikes. A defence name that will not rally on a beat-and-raise INTO a widening war is fully priced. The 'coherent with the supply-shock regime' argument is true and irrelevant if the market refuses to pay for it.

    CUT XLF (11% to 0). It was the one leg with no thesis of its own — its stated job was to supply positive SPY beta so the book was not a pure short-market expression. I am scored on flat dollars, not tracking error, so paying 11 points for beta cosmetics is a waste. It is also the least coherent leg with the mandate: an oil shock at $89 Brent is stagflationary, and the NIM benefit from rising long yields is offset by the credit cost of a squeezed consumer.

    ADD ERX 22% to 32% (64% effective XLE). The single best piece of information I found is that XLE rose 1.88% on a 6.2% crude day. The equity market is pricing this as temporary and crude as mean-reverting; Hormuz has been shut since March and the ceasefire has already failed once. That skepticism is simultaneously my upside (equities have to converge) and my downside cushion (they cannot give back a move they never made — 2026 downside capture on crude down-days was 0.27x). ERX again realised exactly 2.0x with no decay, so I am getting the leverage cleanly. Stop stays at -30%, which caps this leg at 9.6% of NAV and corresponds to roughly a -15% XLE break.

    ADD MPC 9% to 16%. Highest-conviction single name and the only near-dated catalyst I own: 4 August, consensus EPS +184-199% y/y on record cracks, with management having pulled 40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run at 94% utilisation into this window. The sell-side average PT of $301.59 is stale and sits below spot while the two most recent revisions are Goldman $376 and TD Cowen $357. Crack spreads are a genuinely different driver from crude beta (-0.16 correlation to SPY), so this is not just more ERX. I am sizing it BEFORE the print because the print is the reason. The -25% stop caps the leg at 4.0% of NAV, which is the price of admission for a stock up 71% YTD.

    ADD XLY SHORT 13% to 17%. The purest expression of the whole thesis and now doing double duty: $89 Brent is a consumer tax, and 39% of this ETF is AMZN plus TSLA — the two names carrying both the consumer squeeze and the AI-valuation de-rating that took XLK down 6.81% in July. At -0.38 correlation to XLE it is additive to the energy core rather than an offset, and it is my only real protection if the market breaks broadly. An ETF, so no single-name squeeze risk; 3% borrow; stop stays -18%.

    HOLD XLV at 20%. This is what lets me carry an 80% effective energy position. -0.07 correlation to XLE, 13.7% vol, +25% over one year, and State Street just moved healthcare to positive for Q3 on pipeline wins. Still unlevered on purpose — I do not want leverage on the ballast.

    HOLD DOGE short 3% at 3x. Unchanged logic and still free leverage: short perps pay zero funding while longs pay leverage x 10% APR. DOGE is at $0.0702, has not participated in any crypto bounce, and the loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin. Trimmed a point to fund the core.

    RISK FRAME. Effective energy exposure goes from ~53% to 80% of NAV. That is the mandate, executed at the size the new rules permit and the news now justifies. The single risk that kills this book is a durable ceasefire headline, because it hits ERX, MPC and the XLY short simultaneously. I have sized so that scenario is survivable rather than hedged away: with both stops firing the arithmetic bound is roughly -13 to -14% of NAV, against an upside of similar magnitude on a 15% XLE convergence — and I take that as skewed in my favour because energy equities never priced the spike they would have to give back. I am keeping 12% in cash at 4% as genuine dry powder rather than forcing it into the same trade; concentration where I have conviction, cash where I do not, and no third-best ideas in between. Filling on the next trading date — crude has already gapped and the equities have not followed, so I do not want to wait.

  3. 2026-08-03REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_unrestricted.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: One leg of this book was built on reasoning that facts falsified within 24 hours of my writing it, and correcting a wrong thesis is not churn. I wrote that 39% of XLY sat at the intersection of the consumer squeeze and the AI de-rating. Both halves are now false: AMZN posted accelerating 37% AWS growth and rose 15.6% on 7/31, so 23% of my biggest short is an AI winner; TSLA is another 16% and expensive gasoline is a tailwind for EVs, meaning I was short a beneficiary inside an oil-tax trade. And the oil tax itself is easing at the pump — gasoline peaked above $5.00 in mid-June and is now ~$4.27, with ex-gasoline retail spending resilient. That leg has to go, and I am not paying to keep a short whose largest holdings are structurally on the wrong side of my own thesis. I am replacing it with the same trade expressed correctly. Airlines are the direct P&L counterparty to my refiner long: refiners earn the record crack, airlines pay it, jet fuel is +130% y/y at up to a quarter of opex, Spirit is already gone and the $2.5bn budget-carrier bailout has been publicly rejected by the administration — yet JETS trades near the top of its 52-week range. Second change: the evidence for refining margins hardened materially while the evidence for crude-beta convergence did not. Valero reported after I set this book, beat by 27%, and guided Q3 capture rates ABOVE Q2 on cheaper feedstock, against an all-time-high 3-2-1 crack. That driver is refinery capacity shortage, not Hormuz, so it partly survives the ceasefire headline that is the single scenario that kills this book, whereas 2x crude beta does not. So I move six points out of ERX into VLO and keep the energy weight roughly where it was while shifting its centre of gravity from the leg I merely believe to the leg that is confirmed. Everything I got right stays untouched: ERX, XLV, MPC and the DOGE perp keep their sizes and stops, and I pay no cost on them. Cash rises to 17% deliberately — not indecision but the only real hedge against a durable ceasefire, held at 4% with MPC printing Tuesday as a live reason to deploy it.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I am exiting refining entirely because the thesis was falsified by the people who run the companies. I sized MPC at 16% on the specific premise that management front-loaded ~40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 to run flat-out into this window, and I added VLO at 10% because its CEO had guided Q3 margins above Q2 with the binary print already behind it. On the 4 August call MPC told me Q3 carries ~$290mn of turnaround expense plus planned conversion-unit maintenance, that Q3 historically averages 95% capture against the 112% just printed, that early-Q3 margins are 'not at Q2 levels', that the jet-to-diesel spread has narrowed and that some Q2 drivers were 'not repeatable'. That is my sizing premise reversed by the issuer. The tape says the same thing louder: a 27% EPS beat ($17.73 vs $13.95, $5.1bn net income, margin doubled to $36.33/bbl) and the stock closed 8/7 at $301, below the ~$314 where I bought it. When a print that good cannot lift a stock, the forward money has already left. The commodity confirms it — the 3-2-1 crack's all-time $70-72 was a July peak, NY Harbor diesel has fallen from 84c on 10 July to ~60c and is now below its five-year average, distillate exports set an all-time weekly record, and EIA looks for significantly narrower cracks in 4Q26. Holding a token position with a dead thesis is worse than holding none, so both go. Second, Friday's payrolls print (-23k vs +80k, with ~100k of downward revisions to May and June, wage growth at a 2021 low) is a genuine regime break: an oil-driven inflation impulse landing on a contracting labor market. That is demand-negative for exactly the refined products I just sold, and it re-prices the Fed from a possible hike to cuts. The asset that wins in both tails of my own book is precious metals — it gets the haven bid if Hormuz escalates and the rate-cut bid if the strait reopens into a weakening economy — so gold becomes my largest single position at 20% with silver at 7% for beta to the same call. I take this in bullion, not miners: GDX/GDXJ have been squeezing shorts violently, which tells me the direction is right and the entry is extended, and I do not need levered operating gearing stacked on top of a 2x energy fund. Third, I keep the energy core because it is the one leg the week actually confirmed — crude fell ~5% and XLE gave up only ~1.5%, XLE rose 1.48% on Friday against a down tape, and energy is still the best-performing US sector. But 26% of a 2x fund is a 52% effective single-sector bet, and the de-escalation path is no longer a headline, it is a draft accord sitting in the Iranian parliament. Trimming to 20% keeps 40% effective XLE as my largest risk exposure while the labor data resolves. XLV goes up rather than down because the defensive rotation is now the trade and not merely the ballast — it closed 8/7 at $165.68 near a 52w high of $168.53, +29% on the year, 0.56 beta, and it is explicitly being bought as the haven for money leaving tech. JETS comes down to 6%: the demand half of the short improved on Friday but the cost half is going the wrong way, and I have the June precedent that a fuel-price drop puts 6-7% into airline stocks in one session. It is a labor-rollover short now, not a fuel-cost short, and it is smaller because it stays directionally additive to whatever energy exposure I still carry. Total turnover is roughly 65% one-way at ~2bps a side, about 1.3bps of NAV — cheap enough that being wrong for another week costs far more than the trade does.

Cheap convexity and convexity worth buying are different claims. I also tested swapping into VIXM and rejected it: VIXM delivers 1.92% on SPY's worst days against VIXY's 7.69%, so matching the payoff needs 4x notional and costs more per unit of protection at 5, 10 and 63 days. So the leg stays exactly as it is, at a size that is honestly a tail hedge rather than a position. Take-profit held at +60% so a moderate scare leaves the hedge intact and only a genuine dislocation converts it to cash. No stop, for the reason that never changes: stopping out of insurance while it is losing money is the one thing insurance must never be allowed to do.

    Outlook at registrationI expect a low-volatility, positively-skewed-in-stress return profile: roughly 8-9% annualized portfolio vol against SPY's 11.65% realized, grinding out carry from the variance premium and the leveraged-ETF decay while the low-vol equity core supplies muted beta. In a continued calm melt-up this book should make money but lag SPY by several points a quarter; in a correlation spike it should be roughly flat to positive while SPY falls, because VIXY's convexity and the short-TQQQ leg both pay. Management at the weekly reassessment is explicitly regime-driven and mechanical: if SPY 20d realized vol rises through roughly 18% or the 10d/60d ratio moves above 1.3, I cut SVXY toward zero, cut the short-gamma pair (trend is its enemy), raise VIXY and cash, and rotate the equity core further toward USMV; if realized vol falls back under 10% with VIX still near 18 I add to SVXY and the decay pair. If dispersion compresses — the implied-correlation proxy climbing back toward 0.55 — the case for holding low-vol equity over the index weakens and I would move the core toward broader beta. The specific thing that would make me abandon the construction is realized vol printing above implied for several weeks, which would mean the premium I am being paid has gone negative.

    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-02-14 to 2025-05-30 (stress)

    Numbers are verbatim from `python3 tracker/round2.py --backtest <entry> <end> <file>` on this exact construction. The engine reports NAV $1041.42 / $1016.88 / $1054.73 on $1000. THE CENTRAL CAVEAT: a static allocation cannot switch regimes mid-window, which is the entire point of the strategy. These three windows therefore test whether the CURRENT regime call (calm index, high dispersion, wide variance premium) would have survived three different historical tapes — they do NOT test the switching rule, which only becomes visible across weekly reassessments in the live round. The book underperforms SPY by 4.6 and 8.2 points in the two rising windows and beats it by 8.5 points in the stress window; that asymmetry is the intended character, not a defect, but it means a sustained melt-up is the most likely way this book finishes behind. STOP DESIGN, FOUND BY ITERATION: an earlier candidate carried 30% stops on both leveraged-ETF legs and returned -5.92% with a -11.20% drawdown in 2026H1, because a whipsaw stopped out first one leg and then the other, twice converting a hedged pair into a naked directional short; removing the per-leg stops took the same window to +1.62% and the stress window from -0.05% to +7.83%. The pair is therefore risk-controlled by SIZE and by the natural floor on a short, not by stops. SVXY's stop was likewise widened from 18% to 25% after the tighter level fired at the March-2026 vol bump and locked in a loss the position then recovered. SHORT-VOL TAIL RISK, STATED PLAINLY: the accepted loss on a 1-day -21% / 5-day -34% SVXY event is about -3 to -4% of NAV after the stop, partly offset by VIXY, and the engine only checks stops at daily closes, so an intraday gap would fill worse than the stop level. In the stress window SVXY hit its stop and VIXY hit its take-profit (the engine prints these closures as LIQUIDATED) and the book still finished +5.47%, which is the hedge working as designed. Other caveats: no market impact or borrow-availability constraint on the leveraged-ETF shorts, flat 3% borrow and 10% funding, and daily-close granularity throughout.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I am not touching the equity core, which is a session old and needs no change; I am closing the two carry legs because one had its premise refuted overnight and the other was already refuted by my own arithmetic. SVXY existed to harvest the gap between implied and realized index vol. When I sized it that gap was ~7 points; after VIX collapsed 22% to ~16 against SPY realized of ~13-14% it is ~2-3 points. Getting paid 2-3 points to be short the tail is thin at the best of times, and this is not the best of times: the 10y just broke to 4.75% on $100 oil and an escalating Middle East conflict, which is precisely the macro shock that drags implied correlation back up and hurts a short-index-vol position most. The carry shrank and the tail fattened simultaneously, so the leg goes. The TQQQ/SQQQ pair is me correcting a documented mistake rather than reacting to news: on 7/30 I wrote that my own backtest gives it ~1.2%/yr on notional against 3% APR borrow on EACH leg — roughly -0.25% of NAV per year with a -27.76% worst 63-day — and then kept it at 7+7 anyway because it 'expressed the regime.' That was attachment to a narrative over my own numbers. It is a negative-carry structure whose best environment is chop and whose worst is trend, and an oil-and-rates shock is a trending catalyst, so the case only got weaker. Closing both costs about 26% turnover at ~2-2.5bps, roughly $0.07, and it is economically positive from day one: I stop paying 0.42%/yr of NAV in borrow and start earning 4% on the cash. VIXY goes up rather than down as the exact mirror of my 7/30 trim — I cut it then because buying insurance at VIX 20.66 right after a pop is paying up post-event, and the same insurance now costs ~22% less in VIX terms while the event it insures against became materially more likely. Buy convexity when it is cheap and the tail is fat; that is the discipline, and it is the reason I can still run an 78% low-vol equity core. The 16% cash is deliberate, not a residual: with my short-vol carry removed and a live geopolitical/inflation catalyst, dry powder that pays 4% is the right way to hold risk in reserve, and it funds adding to the core if the rate shock hands me a better entry. Net result is a simpler book, lower gross, no borrow, more cash yield, and my two best-evidenced legs plus a cheap hedge.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two things moved enough to force this, and they point the same way. First, the volatility risk premium has closed: VIX 15.15 against SPY 20d realized 13.49% is ~1.7 points, versus a ~3-4 point norm, so index vol is no longer expensive - and Cboe implied correlation sits at a 23-year low (COR3M ~9-10, 52-week range 9.29-11.95), which is a bounded, mean-reverting quantity that can only normalise upward. Long index vol therefore pays if realized rises OR correlation normalises, and the compressed contango (VX6/VX1 1.062 vs a 1.15-1.20 norm) means I pay a third-to-half the carry I underwrote at entry. Cheaper insurance against a denser calendar - CPI 12-Aug, a stalled Hormuz fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC where a Warsh hike is still 44% priced after payrolls printed -23k with 103k of downward revisions. Second, and this is the correction I owe myself: I have been conflating vol targeting with owning low-vol stocks. Vol targeting scales exposure to the INDEX by the index's realized vol. USMV and SPLV buy their low vol by surrendering expected return and by parking 25% of SPLV in utilities ahead of a live hike; the index buys its low vol from diversification, which is free and is at a 23-year maximum precisely because correlation is at a 23-year low. At COR3M ~10 the S&P realizes 13.5% while its average constituent realizes far more - that makes SPY the cheapest carrier of equity risk in my universe right now, not USMV. My book was carrying only ~40 SPY-equivalent betas into a low-correlation, low-index-vol tape and made +0.97% while the index made +3.58% and tech made +7.2%. The fix is not to abandon defence, it is to take the permission the insurance already bought: raise index beta and raise the hedge together. Modelled across three states - calm melt-up, moderate scare, and a VIX-doubling shock - the new shape beats the old one in every one, because more cheap convexity is what makes more beta affordable rather than a substitute for it.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two pieces of my own evidence turned against last week's construction and one turned against last week's arithmetic, so this is a correction rather than a view change - the regime call (calm index, violent components) is unchanged and this book expresses it better.

    First, the arithmetic. I built a 40% SPY core on 'index variance equals average constituent variance times correlation', arguing the cap-weighted wrapper is safer than its contents at a 23-year correlation low. That identity is an equal-weight identity. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%, on the same tape in the same window - the equal-weighted index captures the diversification benefit I was describing while SPY's megacap concentration consumes most of it. I checked this was not a 20-day artefact before acting on it: over the trailing year RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% with a smaller max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture across SPY's eight worst days. Identical return, a quarter less volatility, at all three horizons. If my mandate is return per unit of realized vol, RSP is simply the better vehicle for the exact thesis I already hold, so 30% moves to RSP and SPY keeps 20% because I am correcting an expression, not abandoning cap-weighted beta entirely.

    Second, the carry. VIXM/VIXY moved +3.9% in five sessions against a ~1.1%/week three-month average; netting each ETF's beta to spot leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. On 08-08 I explicitly justified upsizing VIXY to 11% on the claim that compressed contango had cut my roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr underwritten at entry. That claim is now false by my own measurement. Separately, the value case has thinned: VIX 14.25 against 10d realized 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium, near normal, and realized is falling faster than implied. I am not abandoning the hedge - VVIX at 87 is cheap convexity, SKEW rose to 138 in a week VIX fell, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC is a dated live binary inside my horizon - but a leg whose price of carry has doubled while its value case thinned should shrink to true insurance size, so 11% goes to 7% with the take-profit untouched.

    Third, SPLV. I kept it for tech-free diversification, but its protection is a rates bet and rates went the wrong way: ^TNX to 4.70 with ^IRX pinned at 3.70, a long-end-led steepening, which is precisely the inflation-expectations move an +7.9% Brent week produces. XLU -2.55% and SPLV -0.57% on the month confirm it. Once RSP is in the book, SPLV's broad-diversification role is redundant and only its concentrated utilities bet remains, so I exit it.

    What replaces it is the reason I am comfortable cutting the vol sleeve. XLE printed positive on five of SPY's eight worst days of the trailing year - better crash behaviour than SPLV's four of eight - while returning +49.2% over that year against SPLV's +6.2%. It is long the one macro shock actually running (Brent +7.9%, XLE +7.7%, USO +7.3% in a week the S&P gained 0.4% and VIX fell), and an energy-led inflation impulse is the single state where SPY, USMV and cash all lose together and only my hedges help. Sized at just 7% because it realizes 24.5% vol and because a leg that ran 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect, not enthusiasm. The net effect is a book with the same equity beta, materially less realized volatility, a hedge that earns rather than bleeds, and 18% cash at 4% into a live September Fed.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The regime call was right and paid - the book made +0.30% while SPY lost 1.37% - so this is not a view change. It is a correction of where the hedge sits. I built this book to be hedged against an energy-inflation shock and then measured, for the first time, what each leg actually does when that shock arrives: regressed on daily 30y yield changes and ranked against the twelve largest yield-up days of the year, XLE is the ONLY long leg I own with positive rate beta (+1.86%/10bp at 60d, 8/12 positive, avg +0.72%), while SPY is -0.57, RSP -0.91 and USMV -0.40. The risk I named is now the one actually running - the 30y printed 5.31% this week, a 19-year high, on fiscal supply and term premium rather than policy - and I was carrying 7% against it and 68% exposed to it. Two dated catalysts sit inside the horizon and both push the same way: Bessent's Iran measures Monday 08-24 with Brent already +13% over two weeks on persistent Hormuz shut-ins, and Warsh's debut Jackson Hole keynote Friday 08-28, where September is now priced ~1-in-3 for a HIKE with three standing dissents already voted for one. So I double the macro hedge to 15% and fund it by trimming SPY from 20% to 14%, which is the same trade twice: a term-premium shock is a discount-rate shock and it hits the longest-duration cash flows hardest, which is precisely SPY's ~40% megacap concentration - XLK -3.53%, SMH -4.66%, Meta -7% in a week SPY lost 1.37% and RSP lost 0.49%. That is a mechanism, not the leadership forecast I said last week I did not have. I split the hedge across XLE and COMT rather than loading XLE alone because ~15% of XLE is refiners whose crack spreads can compress on exactly the transit-disruption shock I am hedging, and because XOM+CVX are 35% of the fund. Backtested over the trailing year the new book returns +14.02% against the current book's +11.83% at 5.03% vol vs 4.86% and -2.34% max drawdown vs -2.11%, with a better ten-worst-day average (-0.25% vs -0.37%) - more return, better crash behaviour, marginally more vol, and every variant I tested beat the incumbent, so the improvement is robust to the exact weights rather than fitted to them. VIXY stays at 7% despite finding the cheapest VIX convexity in two years (VVIX 2nd percentile, VIX minus rv20 at the 27th percentile against a 4.11 mean): I ran the sizing test before acting and across a year containing ten sessions worse than -1.5%, every extra point of VIXY above 7% cost more carry than it returned. Turnover is ~14% of NAV at 2bp a side, under a basis point all in.

Web search budget was exhausted session-wide, but WebFetch against Yahoo Finance/stockanalysis pages worked and gave live prices + 1mo/3mo/6mo trailing performance plus embedded news snippets as of 2026-07-29/30 close. Key findings: an AI-capex/semis unwind is in full swing -- SMH -20.2% 1mo (-4.8% just on 7/29), SOXL (3x) -61.1% 1mo, described in press as 'the chip crash exposing the brutal cost of leverage.' CAT is down -24.2% 1mo (-6.9% on 7/29) after a Baird downgrade citing regulatory pushback on data-center power-generation demand -- i.e., CAT got hit by the same AI-capex backlash it was supposed to benefit from as a broad industrial-capex play. XLI -1.2% 1mo (-3.2% on 7/29) and IWM -3.5% 1mo are both soft amid the broader risk-off spillover. On the other side, FXI is up +12.9% 1mo (EM/China rotation working cleanly), GLD +0.7% 1mo and holding above $4000/oz spot despite a rough prior quarter (dollar-debasement/safe-haven thesis intact), XLV +7.3% 1mo and XLF +7.5% 1mo are both strong (healthcare/financials rotation firmly confirmed), XLY -1.65% 1mo/-7.6% 3mo (discretionary laggard short thesis working), and SOL-USD is roughly flat 1mo (-0.6%) but still down -37.7% 6mo (momentum breakdown thesis intact but stalled short-term). Could not confirm the exact July FOMC outcome (Fed press-release page had no accessible decision text, CNBC blocked, search budget exhausted) so I treated the equity action as AI-capex-driven rather than a confirmed dovish/hawkish surprise. Net read: both books' short-AI-infra/semis legs and dollar-debasement/rotation legs are working strongly and get sized up; the capex-linked cyclical longs (CAT especially) and the biotech long (XBI, which has rolled over) get cut or trimmed.
